en: There was a king named Daśaratha, a friend of the gods, a scorcher of enemies, and endowed with sacred learning;
he was preeminent in virtues, and the Eternal One himself came to him as his father under the guise of benefiting the world.
He studied the Vedas,
performed sacrifices for the gods,
and supported his ancestors.
He honored his kinsmen,
conquered the sixfold group [of sense-faculties], delighted in statesmanship,
and destroyed his enemies along with their very roots.
He manifested treasures and water like a rain-cloud; he sat upon his throne with the mountain-splitter (Indra);
she did not worship anyone other than Tryambaka (Śiva).
His glories eclipsed those of all living beings;
that king, who was a mass of merit, honored by the assembly of Great Brahmas, a source of satisfaction for the inhabitants of heaven, and most excellent,
blazed for the stability of the world like the fire consecrated at a sacrifice.

That Puṇyakīrti, equal to Indra in his splendor, inhabited the city of Ayodhyā— which was like the world of Mahendra in its prosperity and free from disease and pleasant in all seasons— along with Brahmins whose awakening was radiant.
He was as if the very limit of the skill of the Lotus-Seated One (Viṣṇu) in the art of emanation, regarding all that he desired.
Where the city of Indra stands as if laughing, with upward-shooting rays from its jeweled radiance;

where the houses, possessing fine gems, pearls, and diamonds, and featuring various minerals along with groves, are filled with women like throngs of celestial nymphs, resembling the peaks of Mount Meru.
In that city, from the houses, the light of brilliant jewels set within them issues forth through the lattice-windows like the falling waters of the Gaṅgā from the peaks of the snowy mountains;
and at the proper time, righteous ways— conducive to pleasure, wealth, and fame, and esteemed by the world— are practiced.

Like a scholar among the sciences, that king took delight in his three excellent wives. Desiring a son, he brought from afar a learned and ritual-performing sage, one whose understanding had reached maturity through study, who was wise, venerable, and a seer named Ṛṣyaśṛṅga; and the sage entered his own city.

The king, having prepared himself, approached that Lord of Sages to have him perform a sacrifice for the fruit of obtaining a son; then the Sage, whose mind was a reservoir of wisdom, being diligent in his task, performed the rite resulting in a daughter.
He drove away the Rākṣasas from around the altar, offered the limbs of the animal, and then sacrificed the principal victim.
The most excellent one, having offered the remaining oblations for the sake of his son's prosperity,
requested a boon from the king.
When the artificial joy and fear had come to an end following the performance of the prescribed rites, the king’s wives...
Those of noble lineage, who had consumed the remnants of sacrificial offerings, gave birth to four excellent sons. First, Rāma was born easily by Kausalyā; thereafter, Bharata was born from Kaikeyī.
Sumitrā, of noble conduct, gave birth to Śatrughna along with Lakṣmaṇa.

The learned ascetic Vasiṣṭha, the best among self-controlled men, honored the twice-born who had found the supreme goal, and at the appropriate time, he restrained the hosts of spirits who were causing terror. He also initiated them [in the sacred rites] at the proper time.
The Veda with its limbs was studied in its entirety; victorious weapons were mastered.
Though their modes of conduct differed, those virtuous men dwelt together with minds at peace.
Then, his ritual activities assailed by Rākṣasas, the son of Gādhi approached the lord of the earth.
In order to choose Rāma for the sake of his protection,
the king approached him with the *madhuparka* in hand.
That you have sought [this] for the sake of conquering rebirth—
And because you turned away from the perception of form and so forth,
and by which you realized the various truths,
O King, that meditation he called "Auspicious" (Śiva).
The Sage has proclaimed the auspiciousness of that meditative absorption; yet the *rākṣasas* obstruct it, as they do the sacrifices in the forest.
May Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, trample them down, subduing the prowess of those enemies.
Having heard those words, the king, unable to endure the separation from his son, was bewildered;
then the lord of the earth, full of pride, was addressed with auspicious words by that elephant among ascetics:
"In times of fear, you have found refuge in me."
We have also been obtained by you for the increase of Dharma;
both the Kṣatriya and the twice-born status serve each other's purpose,
so do not entertain any doubt.
Abandon your own son; by him a great adversary will be slain,
and by him [the enemy] who stands before you in battle will be held at bay.
"O Great-Souled One, do not disregard me; one such as I shall not be assigned this foremost burden.
If he becomes angry, the Brahmin-fire will consume my lineage; if he departs, my son, filled with resentment, will cause me grief."
In this manner the king first reflected, and then he gave permission for his son’s departure.
Having honored the lord of the earth with blessings, the sage, being pleased, set out once more for the hermitage.
Following behind him on horseback,

the youthful Lakṣmaṇa— born of three mothers, bold, skilled in all missiles and weapons, and ever devoted to the highest good— went along with his bow drawn and ready against those who would do harm, as he, the victorious Rāma, was proceeding toward the sacred grove with a radiant countenance.
When Raghusiṃha— armed with arrows, desiring to slay the venomous serpents, and grasping his bow with a grip so firm it was unbearable for his enemies—
was proceeding with his finger-guards bound in variegated fashion, the young women of the city, though overcome by heavy grief, somehow refrained from weeping and, instead,
the Brahmins uttered auspicious blessings for him in loud voices.
Others struck musical instruments with a tumultuous sound; his arm throbbed beautifully, foretelling a desired fruit; and favorable birds chirped loudly from the trees.

Emerging from that city, he beheld autumn on all sides before him, bestowing its splendor upon the trees, the lakes, the rivers, the luminous bodies, the radiant directions, and the quarters of space.
Bearing an extraordinary beauty of flames through their trembling petals tossed by the waves,
the red lotuses shone with the luster of smoky, blazing fires, their six-legged bees agitated.
Seeing their own splendor eclipsed by the waters, as the forests on the banks were reflected therein, [the lotuses appeared to weep].
The banks of the lake extended the splendor of their lotuses through the smiles of land-lotuses, as if out of indignation [at the night's departure].

At the break of day, the tree on the shore, with clear drops trickling from the edges of its leaves— drops resembling tears shed for the frost of the night— and with its birds singing, seemed to weep for the lily pond.
With their eyes like the forest groves and the waters, and with lotuses upon which bees were settled,
they gazed at one another’s splendor with wonder and great respect, as it were.
The form of the night-lily plant, its body turned tawny by the pollen of the flowers, was trembling violently from the morning breeze.
Like a lotus plant when it is angry, she casts away the bee; a proud woman does not tolerate the company of another.
Desiring to kill a deer that has fixed its attention on the song of a honey-licking [bee] and whose movements have become still, [the hunter...]

Hearing the eager cries of the swans, the deer could not maintain its concentration on the target. On the mountain slope, a cloud— shattered by the wind, white as snow, and containing only a remnant of water—
enhanced the beauty of the Lord of Mountains by swelling the headwaters of the rivers.

Roaring in the water amidst the mountain thickets, the lion heard the echoes produced by himself; suspecting them to be the cries of another king of beasts, he became enraged and halted his stride as he prepared to leap.
He then beheld the waters filled with fresh blue lotuses.
He heard the songs of the bees;
he smelled the fragrant breeze carrying the scent of the lotuses with which it was in contact;
and he gathered flowers as they fell from the creepers.
Having bathed at the river crossing,
the descendant of Kakutstha sat upon a beautiful stone, smiling slightly out of curiosity.
At dawn, he saw the waters before him not far away, suffused by the rays of the sun;
they appeared like streams of light from the sun’s beams, as if the very brilliance of the sun had been gathered upon the earth.
Spreading across the quarters, captivating to the eye, and following from purification, they seemed to pour forth oil.

He rejoiced at seeing rows of excellent grain, straight and long, with the spaces between them free of weeds. He beheld the cow-pens filled with men who were honest and devoid of artificial splendor, who gave their king’s share at the proper time, being themselves ignorant of the experience of the pain of separation.

He rejoiced at beholding the women of the cowherds: their feminine ornaments, their modest gestures, their beautiful and sidelong glances, and their upright natures that inspired confidence. He beheld them as they turned their sides, performing graceful movements of the limbs, beautiful with their lovely hips.
The dancing of the cowherd women, which kept time with the deep and rhythmic sound of churning, delighted him.
From nearby, a herd of deer, startled by curiosity, leaped high and in various ways, spreading a wondrous spectacle that surpassed the beauty of the forest regained at the end of the rainy season.

And rows of kalahamsa geese, white as kunda flowers, resting upon clusters of white lotuses and on sandy banks covered with tangled reeds, were perceived by their cries that brought delight to the ears.
That was no mere water;
That which is not a very beautiful lotus is not a lotus if it has no bees alighting upon it.
That is not a six-legged bee which does not hum sweetly; nor is that a humming which is not [sweet].

Those who performed sacrifices along with the foremost of monks, emaciated by asceticism and carrying jars of water for peace in their hands, as well as other forest-dwellers with flowers and fruits— these venerable ones honored him, who is worthy of worship by the entire world, though he did not captivate their minds.
Then, with his soul unimpaired, the son of Gādhi duly taught him the *Vijayā* and *Jayā* spells in order to cast down the hosts of *rakṣasas*, intending to strike down the *yātudhānas* in battle;
[he taught] that collection of unfailing weapons for one who would stand firm in the fray against the approaching great conflict.
The Sage, ever vigilant for his own welfare, gave [the bow] to him for the slaying of the night-stalkers.
A night-stalker woman, having made an effort to kill that Brahmin as he was walking through the forest, approached him;
Rāma, knowing her intent to kill and wielding a radiant weapon, slew her, who was named Tāḍakā.

Then he beheld the penance grove, its branches thick and glossy as if with the collyrium of the flames of sacrificial smoke; it resounded with the beautiful warbling of birds whose wings were stirred by the chanting of sacred hymns. There, the lions did not devour the small deer.
It was filled on all sides with flocks of birds;
there, the swaying creepers shone as if bowing down out of a desire to bestow their fruit.
The foremost forest-dwellers, skilled in hospitality, honored him with seats, water for his feet, and garlands.
The two sons of the protector of the earth accepted from him the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and other offerings, including seats.
"You two have borne the burden of the world with your arms when it was oppressed by the Daityas and sinking;
even now, protect the sacrificial oblations."
Those two spoke thus to the ascetics.
Then Rāghava replied to them: "The righteous task you have proposed is exactly as desired."
"May the heat of your asceticism become for you a fire of arrows; let it be kindled upon the fuel of our enemies.
Then they praised the ritual action with the various sacrificial materials prepared according to rule.
That which was performed by the officiating priests as directed by Dakṣiṇya spread forth and was perceived by the Yātudhānas.
Then the night-stalkers, with their tawny and coarse hair standing erect on their heads, and with veiny legs reaching as high as mountain peaks,
filled the sky with their broad, tawny eyes, like clouds of the rainy season.
With his bowstring drawn, his grip firm upon the bow, his eyes wide and rolling, and his right thigh raised, [he stood ready].
Lakṣmaṇa, whose left leg was bent, struck them with arrows drawn slowly from his pure quiver. Rāma too, skilled in illusory weapons and proficient in missiles,
spoke these words of great significance in a loud voice to Mārīca— who was roaring like a bull as directed by Gādheya— as he stood firm in battle with a smiling face.
You, who support yourself alone, take the flesh of men and strike down the lords of the forest for their fruit;
why do you not feel compassion for those whose wealth does not even last until tomorrow?
We shall slay the twice-born, we shall kill those who sacrifice to the gods, and we shall turn the city into an abode for departed spirits and outcasts.
"O son of Daśaratha, this dharma is indeed our own; we have never acted contrary to the Vedic way of life.
It is true that you possess dharma, O Rākṣasa, but another dharma also extends to me."
"I shall slay those haters of the Veda with this [weapon],
for I am one who maintains the conduct of a Kṣatriya, bearing my bow and arrows.
Thus did Rāma and the Night-stalker (Rāvaṇa) engage in combat, making such proclamations in battle.
Then, regarding him as a mere blade of grass, the son of Raghu dispatched the Rākṣasa from the battle with an arrow.
The minds of the twice-born became serene,
and the sky became intent on raining down heaps of flowers.
A sincere sacrifice was performed, and the sage spoke further to the prince:

"O Hero, this earth, though adorned with the thunderbolt-weaponed [Indra] and presided over by you— who have utterly conquered the devouring [demons] at the divine sacrifice— is filled with shame before even heaven."
Bali was bound, the ocean was churned, and the nectar was seized.
"He has conquered the race of Daityas;
likewise, he bore the earth which was distressed at the end of the eon—thus, this exceedingly heavy burden is not too much for him.
Speaking these sweet and beneficial words, he [the sage] led him to the sacrificial ground of the King of Mithilā.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Sage, with a joyful mind, desiring to seize the fame of the kings, spoke to Rāma:
"Are these Mitra and Varuṇa? Or are they the Aśvins, thirsty for the essence of Soma?"
Those two lions among men surpassed all the people dwelling in Janaka’s hermitage with their beauty.
Janaka presented him with that bow by which the wielder of the Pināka had pierced the city of the Daityas;
desiring to test the strength of his arms, the joy of the Raghus broke it while smiling.

Then the preeminent mortal of Mithilā, desiring to give his daughter to the lord of the earth, dispatched messengers on swift war-horses to call him from Ayodhyā to the mountain passes, where travelers were bathing in the rivers. Thereupon, traveling rapidly on a horse along the road, the king— though most aged— proceeded like a youth.
Having heard of the conduct of the son from the narrators, he traveled to Mithilā on a carriage that did not cause fatigue.
He honored that most beloved one— who was most venerable like a preceptor,
a worthy great soul, the abode of merit, possessed of most abundant fame, and preeminent in glory— among the lords of the earth.
"O Lord, having mastered the three goals of life and having occupied this single throne,
you have attained the state of being the sovereign of the gods who perceive the truth of solitude.
To him, the King of Mithilā spoke these words:
Like a golden *sāla* creeper come to life, or like the stationary radiance of lightning descended from heaven,

the daughter of Mithilā— whose form was as if the presiding deity of the moon’s luster— was given by him to his son. Having obtained her, Rāma, whose conduct is for the benefit of all people, took her as his own wife.
Increasing the splendor of the Raghu lineage with the beauty of the six gems, pearls, and gold,

that army— rich in cavalry, chariots, and elephants— proceeded on its journey toward Ayodhyā along with the king; it was greeted with great joy by those who had arrived at the break of dawn and was praised by those who came to pay homage.
Broad-chested, with arrows in hand, and standing two palm trees tall before him, the formidable Rāma, son of Jamadagni, approached on the road holding his bow, reaching down to his knees.
From afar, he challenged that descendant of Raghu, saying: "Draw this bow with its arrow; you shall not pass me by!"
Knowing his valor and fond of his lineage, the humble lord of the earth, wishing to conciliate him, said:
"O Father, you have conquered many kings,
yet you have not offered the blood of those monarchs as water for your ancestors."
Having briefly summarized the intense hostility of his adversaries, [the poet asks]: "O Rāma, what reliance can there be on this child?
When he, out of pride, did not heed the words of Daśaratha..."
Then the prince drew his bow, which held a heavy arrow within,
and he pierced the targets that had been set by the world.
Once the enemy king was defeated,
the various shouting armies, becoming calm and free from fear, entered their many different paths with the consent of the aged king.
Then, through its application of extreme speed, drawing near that which was situated far away and traversing the divisions of the earth with exceeding velocity,
tireless, insentient, and having rendered the ground free of dust,
let it swiftly bring strength and splendor to Ayodhyā.
Through the slaughter in battle of the flesh-eaters and by the defeat of the Destroyer of Kṣatriyas,
the Prince became wealthy and renowned; there was no one who did not hold him dear.

Then, having made his citizens and servants well-disposed, the lord of the earth proclaimed at no low volume, "I shall consecrate my son in the kingdom," and once again made the entire world joyful. He then commanded that the lion throne, together with its footstool, which was like a blazing fire, be prepared for him.
[He] set in place beautiful vajras of refined gold and highly precious jewels arranged in their proper divisions.

He diligently dispatched men with firm bodily frames, carrying jars for the water-offering, who were gathered in groups, questioned regarding their own livelihood, and were quickly wading through the waters at the bathing ghats from all sides.
They prepared the roads of the city with sprinkled water, hoisted banners,
and released incense into the air.

And skilled officials appointed by the king scattered various flowers in all directions for his sake; meanwhile, Kekayī, unable to endure that Bharata had gone to his maternal grandfather’s residence without being asked at that time, demanded Rama’s departure for the forest.

Whispered into his ear by those who had instilled greed for the kingdom, and led to a state of corruption by his weakness for women, he failed to consider the fault of public scandal or the death of the king himself during Rāma’s exile; yet the king, while still professing his intent to restore wealth and territories, was merely speaking of Rāma.
By that [thought], he recognized [the truth],
and the consecration for Bharata, as well as the stake of despondency, were driven deep into his mind.
Then, wishing to lead the prince into the wandering life, he instructed him regarding the departure for the forest.
The king, grieving, traveled in a chariot guided by Sumantra, with the son of Sumitrā and Sītā as his companions. Some censured the king for lacking self-control; others wailed aloud with tears.
Others spoke thus of Bharata’s artifice, while another cried out, "Fie on Kaikeyī! [And others said:
"Rāma will depart for the forest tomorrow."

“Because of grief, the people were excessively distressed in their bodies; but the steadfast ones, having cast off their sorrow, set their minds upon following the Prince. As they were about to depart, those two addressed these words to the mourners who had approached them.”
"Why do you grieve here at our prosperity? Alas! We have fulfilled our father's purpose by obtaining this office—he who created us and he who protected us from dangers."
He who has always nourished us with his own sustenance—
what is the use of a trifling vehicle for one who has been so greatly benefited? It would be better for him to perish like a flash of lightning than to be lost through such a [lesser] liberation.
Or rather, he withered away like grass drying up from the top;
for what need is there to speak of his being far from home? He who had not remained steadfast in the teaching of his gurus addressed the citizens, saying, "Turn back!"
“May he be the dispeller of my father’s grief;
let him not see anyone other than me and Bharata,” the charioteer was thus told by him as he commanded the chariot to turn back.

Having perceived through gestures that people are subject to transience, Rāma, having stayed for a single night with his citizens, departed at dawn under a pretext, protecting them from the fear caused by dwelling in the forest. Wailing piteously, they discharged their tears like a weapon.

Sighing repeatedly with hot breaths and crying out, "Alas, Rāma! Alas, what misery!", they turned back with their minds averse [to the journey]. The charioteer as well, filled with no small measure of grief, purified himself along with the horse by means of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Reciting the account of the two descendants of Raghu along with Sītā, he entered the city breathing hot sighs.

That city, when looked upon by the people, appeared like the sky deprived of both the sun and the moon; though still joined by the constellation of the royalty, its every activity was paralyzed by the darkness of grief.
Having looked for Sumantra and found him without Rāma, the lord of men lost his resolve and despaired; he took no honey, did not anoint himself with perfumes,
and did not clothe himself in beautiful garments.
He did not remain in one place due to his grief;
he desisted from the duties of a protector of the earth, whether performed or left undone.
Anointed with sandalwood, *uśīra*, and lotus stalks, he passed away through the fire of sorrow to dwell in heaven.
The queens of the lord of the earth wailed aloud,
tore at their hair, and beat their own bodies.
They cast off their ornaments,
fell upon the ground,
and even broke their bracelets.
Consoling them and awaiting Bharata, Kausalyā quickly cast him into oil out of affection for her kinsman;
and the king, desiring to bring back his son, dispatched young messengers according to the counsel of his ministers.
"While he was asleep, he beheld the sun fallen from the sky and quivering below."
While residing in his mother’s family, Bharata told his friends of the negligence he observed in the king;
and when messengers arrived and announced that urgent matters required him to depart,
Bharata, longing for his elders, then set out with a desire to go.
He did not fear for his kinsmen because they were overwhelmed by distress, nor for himself because he was under the sway of affection; meanwhile,
the packs of jackals and deer neither retreated properly nor let out their terrifying cries.

Having been away on a journey, as he was about to enter the city upon his return, he did not hear the clamor produced by the throngs of people; he did not listen to the sounds of the Vedas, nor did he perceive the bargaining cries of merchants.

The mothers, having approached the king and come close to him with tears, wailed aloud; so too did the warriors led by the domestic priest and the ministers, their neck-tendons filled with swelling rage.
When he, desiring to see Rāma together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, could not behold them anywhere around him, [he cried out].
Weeping bitterly, he then questioned him, and he related the events to him exactly as they had occurred.
With his brows knit into a terrifying frown and his reddish, fierce eyes rolling in rage, he spoke.
He rebuked Kaikeyī loudly and repeatedly sank down in unceasing grief; meanwhile,
the two sons of the king, together with Sītā, suffered greatly.
The king has died; you have become widows; we are to be pitied.
"O kings of the earth! Alas, this insignificance first introduced by Kekayī brings much misfortune.
Saying, "This is not my view," he swore oaths by the thousands.
While being cremated, he rolled upon the ground with his father and Rāma, weeping aloud in grief. As the ministers sought to comfort the king, they carried him away from the scene;
together with the brahmins, they desired to offer the final oblation and intended to collect the various vessels required for the sacrifice.
Raising aloft banners of fine silk and dukūla cloth, they sounded flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, and bronze gongs;
blowing conchs with piercing sound on all sides,
they likewise brought saffron and sandalwood.
Having covered the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth with gold leaf and placed [the body] upon a deerskin with its head facing east, he—

having reflected and prepared the ritual vessels according to the rules— had the officiating priests offer oblations into the blazing funeral fire. Once the offerings of rice-balls and water had been performed, [he departed].
Having abandoned the consecration prepared by the subjects,
Bharata, desiring to bring Rāma back through persuasion, set out for the forest together with the citizens.
People, hurrying along and pervading the quarters of the sky, arrived and crowded the path.
Even though they were overcome by grief, they shone forth brilliantly with chariots drawn by the lords of serpents, as well as elephants and horses.
The forests were laden with flowers and fruits; they bathed in the waters and gladdened their ancestors.
Having waded across without hesitation, they rested, taking refuge in the shade of the sandbanks.
Having reached the bank of the river Tamasā, they partook of the purity resulting from contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
They went to bathe in the meritorious waters of the Yamunā, their weary movements having been stilled.
They proceeded to the hermitage of the sage Bharadvāja,
where Rāma had rested upon his arrival.
Having fallen away from food, their thirst overflowing despite the abundance of fruits, they were refreshed by cool waters.
Those who were silent, sleeping on the bare ground, constantly striving for yoga and seeking liberation,
prostrated with humility before the sage Bharadvāja and his disciples as he taught them.
For him who desired to attain final nirvāṇa, the wish-fulfilling trees bore fruit through the power of his yoga;
garments of great luster, endowed with softness and exceeding length, were brought forth; and they awaited his command.
They approached with modesty, sang with passion, and danced with graceful gestures.
Tilottamā and the other women bowed before him with graceful movements and offered him magnificent gifts.
Then, having prepared various garments, food, drink, and bedding according to their respective tastes in suitable locations, the Sage, filled with joy, said to them: "Take your seats; eat and drink."
"Drink!

Eat! Be seated! Having eaten, and having dwelt in great comfort, they put on their garments; and after spending the night, at dawn, they quickly set out on their journey by chariot, horse, and elephant, and reached the Mandākinī with its lovely forests.

Having heard news of Rāma from the forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasas*), they then rejoiced toward Mount Citrakūṭa, whose peaks licked the clouds, which obstructed the path of the sun, and where flocks of birds warbled.
Having seen the floods of his army filling the quarters, he stretched his Śārṅga bow and donned his armor.
Desiring to engage in combat with sharp arrows, the son of Sumitrā stood there, his brows and eyes rising;
but the son of Daśaratha, wearing a white upper garment and bearing no weapons, slowly approached those wrathful men on foot who were coming toward him,
and he perceived them— those whose hostile thoughts had vanished— as his own kinsmen seeking to pay him homage.

Wailing with the force of their grief intensified, they sought out Rāma to uproot him by the very roots; crying out loudly to the protector of the earth that he was dead from the sorrow of separation from Rāma,
they wept piteously and loudly for a long time, and having reached the river named Gotrā, they gathered there.
In the midst of the water, Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa offered two handfuls of water near the waters.
"In the forest journey, my father employed you in what was easy; alas, in the kingdom, he employed you in what is difficult."
"Do not succumb to grief, O hero;
bear this burden," thus spoke the younger brother to Rāma.
“O wise one, skilled in learning and mature in the minds of the elders, if you were not to follow the word of your ancestors,
how could there be a desire for sons here, even when the lineage of another man is being severed?
If you hold in high regard what has been said by us,”
If you have authority over me while I am still alive,
and if you would feel ashamed were I to remain [in disobedience] to my father’s word, then cast away your doubt.
"Go,
rule the earth.
[He replied,] "How could I, the younger brother, venture to bear the burden of sovereignty intended for the eldest legitimate son?"
"Do not compel me to bring about the ruin of my family's reputation," Bharata said to Rāma with steadfastness.
"This [kingdom] is powerful, abounding in elephants and horses."
“O Lord of the Earth, while you remain, these royal jewels and this circle of nobles shall belong to me; thus all is peaceful.
To him who had spoken thus, Rāghava said: “Go, Bharata!”
"Taking my two sandals,
with all your doubts dispelled and being honored by the multitudes of people, rule the kingdom of the entire world according to my will. (Bhk 3.56–2,
Bhk 4)
When Bharata had departed, the wise Rāma entered the forest of asceticism;
having been honored there, he went to the Daṇḍaka wilderness. Wandering through the vast forest together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he [proceeded].
By force, the terrifying *rākṣasa* named Virādha seized the one desiring food and carried him off;
though he was difficult even for Death himself to subdue, they uprooted him with his head hanging downward,
broke his two arms, and buried him in the earth.
Then those two tigers among the Raghus proceeded to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga,
which was presided over by the splendor of Brahman and was a refuge for those seeking shelter. There,
in the presence of Rāma, he offered his body as an oblation into the blazing fire.
Having pointed out from afar the hermitage of the sage Sutīkṣṇa, Śarabhaṅga said:
"We remained in the forest thinking, 'You will surely come here';
now you have been seen."
"May it be well with you;
we shall go to the destination won by our own merit," [he said] in that place where fire had become manifest and in the presence of the very sharp sage.
Wandering incessantly among hermitages, he dwelt in a leaf-hut;
residing in forest dwellings upon beds of leaves,
rising from his bed to hunt deer, he moved about as a hospitable host.
Honoring those reciting the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas, and treating them as deities, the possessor of gold enjoyed the finest meat on spits; meanwhile,
he wore tree bark garments covering his entire body that resembled woven cloth.

Armed with arrows, sword, and bow, and clad in armor, he protected the brahmins; having abandoned the *āśitaṅgavīna* regions where sustenance comes from fruits, he, the enemy of serpents, dwelt in those forests free from fear, like a lion.
Worshipping the Sutvanas— who were like a troop of fierce serpents with blazing weapons— he,
the lord of the great Brahmās, frequented the hermitages of the forest-dwellers by means of his assembly-strength.
Reflecting upon [the past] yesterday, today, the day before, and also on other days, he remained there.
The increase and decrease of the lords of sages became a source of affection for him.
Reciting his prayers while standing at the twilight, he remained until the cows had departed; having awakened before the birds at dawn, he paid homage to the sun.
Then, in the leaf-hut, he was seen by the Rākṣasī Abhikā;
disregarding him as one married to another, she stood before the son of Sumitrā.
Possessing eyes reaching to her ears and a waist that bore the marks of [excessive] fasting, she remained there.
With her skin as smooth as a parrot's wing or a lotus petal, she is like the crescent moon at the beginning of the fortnight;
with well-formed feet, two tusks [incisors], a nose, and thighs, and with palms and fingers that are soft, she possesses a broad and firm hip.
Holding her face high, with earrings swaying upon her pure petals,
wearing a garland and a most gracious smile,
she moved about and fell before the best of the Raghus as he gazed upon her, bringing him auspicious joy.
Then Anukā, speaking sweetly, made this request in order to do what was pleasing:
“O Saumitri, come to me; I am full of desire, longing for you, and under your control.”
"Without fear for your fellow travelers, you shall enjoy human life for its full duration.
He said to her: "In this forest of the cow-pen, terrifying with men and women, why do you, whose form cannot be seen even by the sun, wander about so fearless?"
Desiring humans, radiant and possessing divine qualities, you who act like an *apsaras*—how can you wander here independently? O fierce one, look! You are agitated in the forest, devoid of modesty.
How could a married woman not be skilled in making advances toward a lover?
She desired Rāghava as her husband in the leaf-hut, he who was my lord with eyes reaching to his ears like a lovely forest elephant.
He whose body was fashioned from sandalwood,
whose face was made of black bricks,
and whose hands and knees were capable of performing every task in battle.
He who wears a sword at his side for the protection of the weak, and who carries a bow as hard as stone and arrows difficult for others to bear;
he is the victor over those who harm the sacrifice in battle, and the one who causes the lineage of Dharma to flourish in the forest.
"Having obtained from the sages the perpetual freedom from fear regarding [the loss of] wives and cattle," she,
turning back from there, entered Rāma’s hall,
speaking these respectful words: "He has taken me as his wife."
"He is without a wife, while I am proud of being one;
therefore, your husband prospers all the more," said Rāma; "Go to him alone, do not abandon him."
"Like a cow longing for a bull, she approached Lakṣmaṇa,
her mind once again tormented by the onset of the weapons of Love.
As she pressed upon him, the best of the Raghus felt a desire to tear her apart."
Raising his sword, he made his face hideous;
she said, "Surely you did not recognize me by the name Śūrpaṇakhā, for this wound,
which is curable only by a surgeon, was inflicted upon me."
Standing in the sky, she displayed a terrifying form and wailed; desiring to destroy the prowess of her kinsmen,
she lamented repeatedly before the two brothers, Khara and Dūṣaṇa.
Desiring to incite Rama against the two inhabitants of the Daṇḍaka forest,
he said: "The two who were the unfortunate sons of the king have been exiled by their father for the sake of his fortunate son, Bharata."
Behold the conduct of those two!
O Rāvaṇa, lord of my sister,
this destruction of yours by that ascetic is indeed great.
Forgive me,
if it is fitting for you.
[They were] those who wore unadorned, natural garments and ate unhusked fruit.
"Nevertheless, my non-natural attendants have overcome me.
To this, her two brothers replied: "Tomorrow you shall attain the highest good. She said:
"It is for the sake of your honor that I live."
Go, take heart; do not weep.
We devour men day and night even when they are innocent; O timid one, whence could you possibly come?
"That we should endure even those who act with malice toward us.
Then those two, possessing the strength of fourteen thousand, set forth,
accompanied by men armed with axes, bows, spears, and javelins.
Then, as they were charging, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa struck down in battle those with many heads, those with two heads, and those with three heads, using their terrifying arrows.
By them— [the demons] who were cut, broken, bent, crushed, split, and destroyed— [the field was covered].
The earth was filled with those submerged, distressed, and shrinking,
as well as with the wretched; some fell into trembling, others into extreme fever, and some vomited blood.
And no one at all shone forth.
Then, like a deer pursued by a hunter with an arrow in its right flank, or like a thirsty man in a desert facing a direction ablaze with fire, [he fled].
The three-headed one approached the son of Raghu,
who was like the king of birds with its fierce beak;
his entire face mangled by sharp arrows, he was like a mountain whose peaks are shattered by an earthquake.
He instilled fear in the *rākṣasas*, [a fear] equal to the precursor signs of the total destruction of their entire lineage.
Desirous of repelling, desirous of remaining, and desirous of increasing, he advanced toward the enemy in battle.
Khara and Dūṣaṇa moved about, leaping up and enduring [the blows];
with swords, clubs, spears, discuses, arrows, and maces in their hands,
they created a canopy of weapons amidst the darkness of dust on the battlefield.
Then, with sharp iron arrows, those two best of Raghus struck the hunter in his vital organs; having struck down the hunter, those two fools made their two enemies [the demons] like Yama himself.
With her kinsman slain, Śūrpaṇakhā then departed from the forest.
Having reached the assembly of the Rākṣasas on Laṅkā across the ocean, where her husband Rāvaṇa resided, she cried out, overwhelmed with rage; she wept,
calling out the names of her brothers in the presence of Rāvaṇa.
O Hero, those two preeminent rākṣasas who dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest were slain along with their servants and their followers by two men in battle, increasing the earth's prosperity.
Your body was engaged in combat with Śakra, whose domestic priest is Bṛhaspati, and with Kumāra, the commander of the army; yet you were empty— what logic is there in this?
O Lord, if I had not come when my kinsmen were destroyed and ruined,
you would not have known all this while being negligent and weakened by your spies.
One should understand that what is about to be done is the task at hand;
what indeed has been done by others?
Even when harm is inflicted, you are either ignorant or not one who seeks victory.
Surrounded by those gathered for the sake of alms, you were mounted upon a palanquin, negligent,
addicted to drink, leading a life of luxury, and your mind was not set on the ultimate state.
You frequented the sacrificial rites of those who maintained the sacred fires and pressed the Soma, and you visited the various hermitages.
Now Duścyavana has come to consume the portion of the great Indra;
likewise, the *āmikṣā* curd-milk, the *dadhi-kṣīra*, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the medicinal herbs,
and the clarified butter (*haiyaṅgavīna*)— even these the Rākṣasas do not destroy.

Rāma, of youthful lineage, bow in hand, standing upon the earth, slays those who roam the sky— the destroyers of the sacrifice— with arrows like unto Death himself; O deities, flesh must be torn from the lips as the means for accomplishment.
They eat; the Rākṣasas, fearing Rāma, flee in all directions.
Form your intellect like the tip of a blade of Kuśa grass; abandon the state of following your whims, and lead your inherited fortune down through your sons and grandsons.
Having seized by the hand that flickering prosperity which many diligent and skillful companions aspire to, do not breathe a sigh of relief.
Like an unchaste woman longing for union with another man, Fortune, out of curiosity,
gazes at another even while standing near her husband under some pretext.
His beloved wife was a noble lady who moved with the grace of a swan.
Dark-green like a blade of *dūrvā* grass, she is well-proportioned like a banyan tree.
He who does not behold her face,
or does not kiss her lips, [is lost].
He does not hear what has been said; though his senses are restrained, he is deluded.
He is the essence of the objects of the senses.
I consider that joy of his to be a plunge into hell upon the bed with other beloveds;
fie on it! I do not see him.
If you possess that mind which cannot be provoked even by the three worlds, purchase it and become a man of merit. It is not even Indrāṇī [who can do so].
Neither Rudrāṇī, nor Mānavī, nor Rohiṇī, nor Varuṇānī.
“Even Agnāyī is not equal to her in beauty.
The Lord of Rākṣasas replied to her, “Take heart; why do you fear?”
"Abandon your agitation, O night-walker;
you chatterer,
for I am Rāvaṇa!"
Desiring to see me, Hari approached me, but was repelled by my staff-bearer; though eager to receive my command, he was looked upon from afar with a disdainful glance.
Upon my chest, the thunderbolt—its fierce edge shattered—fell like a flame.
The powerful one, though divided into a hundred parts, considers himself to be strong.
Having made the trees of Laṅkā his tethering post, I bound the elephant Airāvata; yet, because he was useless for binding, I cast him down like a blade of grass.
Behold my self-assurance:
even though the darkness in this city has been destroyed by the luster of excellent jewels, the presence of the full moon is always there.

Having had his jewels stolen and his efforts frustrated, he pays tribute to the *rakṣas* in heaven; ashamed, he approaches the daughter of Pūtakratu—does not the breaker of mountains [Indra] feel such shame?
My conflict with Rāma, who possesses incomparable splendor, is unlike that.
“Even so, this causes me shame; nevertheless, I shall strive to restrain him.
Having leaped into the sky, the ten-headed one, traveling as fast as thought, wielded a sharp weapon.
He set out toward Mārīca, who dwelt near the ocean. Having arrived at his abode, he reported that matter to him; then, having heard the news, Mārīca spoke to the Ten-faced One with trembling.
"Disappear from that tiger among the Raghus, O Lord of Rākṣasas,
who is difficult to approach in battle as he holds his bow in hand;
[disappear] from him whom Kārtavīrya brought to a humiliating peace."
That Rāma conquered his slayer, who was renowned throughout the whole world;
Tāḍakā, who could see into his mouth, knows his prowess.
And I, thinking myself a hero, have been cast out from the battle by him who roars like a lion.
You were not experienced by him, nor was he experienced by you;
yet he has been experienced by me.
And by him I would have been experienced [as inferior],
for Rāma was the preeminent among those who wielded weapons; having encountered him, those like me were cast down.
He broke the bride-price at Mithilā in the sacrifice with his bow;
he was well-known as the one who fought together with Khara and Dūṣaṇa through his power;
and he was a performer of sacrifices along with his sons.
In sacrifices, he [was] a protector of vehicles; born of pleasure, drunk on wine, devouring men, wearing garlands,
he played with women beyond Laṅkā.
"Do not begin a conflict with Bali.
Having reviled him as one who was terrified, Rāvaṇa replied:
"If he defeated Rāma when he was already spent, what of it?"
If those who strike others with sticks are adorned by shame and fear when it comes to women, then praise be to that; fie on this world of petty minds!

That Rāma terrified the cowardly one who roared in his own house with arrows—that was not manliness; [rather, it was the act] of one who performs a sacrifice to a false Brahmin. You, however, have [acted differently].

What wonder is it if Rāma broke an old bow that had been stored for a long time and was worn out by insects, in the presence of a mere Kṣatriya? But what of these two heroes among forest ascetics, who have lost all regard for their rival?
What is so surprising if Khara and Dūṣaṇa, full of contempt,
have perished? But you, O fool, are timid and always desire a refuge.
You deny our virtues and constantly praise our enemies;
therefore, O Expander of the Earth, I shall make you fit to have your head cut off.
Or, wishing to seize [me], he will cause harm to me while I dwell in the forest.
To him, whose sword was raised for the strike, Mārīca—desiring to live and moved by fear—replied with conciliation: "I am no enemy to you."
“Becoming a deer, I shall carry off Rāma and Saumitri while they are hunting for deer;
you too, exerting yourself against the enemy, may spread out as far as you wish. Thereupon, that deer made of gold and jewels was filled with wonder.
Appearing right before Sītā, he leaped about, greatly enticing her.
With that deer, the fawn-eyed Maithilī incited Rāma— who possessed a broad chest— to desire the deer-skin, wishing to have it brought to her.
Then, having ensured the safety and well-being of Sītā by entrusting her to Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāma, who possessed the prowess of an elephant, set out in pursuit of the deer;
he went sometimes moving slowly and at other times advancing with great strides.

Beholding the deer of variegated movements, Rāma was struck with wonder. After long tormenting it, Rāma— piercing its vital spots and causing its leap to falter— let out a cry that protected [the world] from the terrifying night-stalker as it howled.
Hearing that roar which resembled a thunderclap, she lamented; perceiving that Rāma had fallen into distress, she set out to go to the son of Sumitrā.
"This brother of yours is crying out like the sound of a rain-cloud born in the monsoon."
“O Saumitri, show your kinship;
protect Rāghava from this fear!
“This is not the roar of Rāma.”
“Like a deer wishing to escape,
[he] has his own [voice] resembling the cry of Rāma,” he said to her.
O timid one, who is capable of enduring in battle the enraged Kākutstha, whose shoulders, throat, and arms are swelling, who covers the quarters with his arrows? What person,
wishing to preserve their body, would desire to play with their life-breaths in the fire of weapons like a deer?
With his big toe hardened by rubbing it against a bowstring, Rāma was intent on death;
who could cause wonder at that Rāma as he terrified his enemies? "Do not be afraid! [he said].
"Your husband shall see you this very day with your purpose fulfilled. "I desire that you go, yet you do not venture to depart."
"You desire to love me," she said to him.
To her who was speaking a falsehood, that best of the Raghus, whose speech is truth, replied:
The self-controlled one emerged, cursing him, saying, "You shall fall into the hands of the enemy.
When he had gone, Rāvaṇa, pure as water and with his teeth cleansed, entered the fire.
Constantly muttering prayers, he should carry a rosary, a clay vessel,
and a water-pot; with a water-strainer and a bowl, and his head clean, he should wrap himself in dyed garments, gather his requisites, and carry a staff.
Though he was a knower of the self studying sacred lore and maintaining the vow of a wandering mendicant,
he spoke with many finger-snaps, knit his brows, and looked about,
desiring to display his mastery of the *Sāman* chants and wishing to cast off his state of being a beggar.
Having returned from her walk, she said to Sītā, “Be at ease.
With a pure smile, she— whose constant radiance puts to shame the splendor of lotuses that bloom by day after their evening glory has faded— approached.
"Who are you, O timid one, all alone in this forest where no kin remain? Even though the predatory beasts are hungry, why do they not devour you who are unprotected?"
"O you whose form is heart-stealing, why do you say that this forest— which makes even this [place] auspicious— is terrifying?
O you who perform good deeds, whom do you please when you stand near as a protector?"
O you who perform meritorious deeds, who is this flatterer, your servant in matters of pleasure?
This form of yours, which is difficult to find even from the ocean of worlds up to the realm of light, has been seen by us;
because we have beheld it, our lives have become truly lived.
Like a lotus pond on a beautiful day, frequented by bees that have drunk its honey and possessing the splendor of a fine fragrance— my conviction is that you are not a manless woman.
In vain does this "Glorious One" (Śrī) consider herself glorious.
O glorious Manyu, Hari is false;
having directly perceived you, who carry away the glory of Śrī, I consider you to be Śrī herself.
He would not have yearned excessively [for her].
If Smara had beheld you,
he would not have dwelt constantly sporting nor remained united with Rati; and seeing you moving so gracefully, what woman here would not feel resentment?
Who, even one as motionless as a pillar, would not take pleasure in your splendor? All people suffer,
yet you alone find happiness.

"Who was this wise man who, though you were longing for him and did not turn away from his presence, took you— who are like a baited lure— and, fearing those who would treat you as an enemy, dwelt with you in the empty forest?"
While she was being honored, Janaka’s daughter prepared an offering for him and spoke these words with reverence and a faltering voice to the ten-headed one:
"O noble-born descendant of Ikṣvāku, you are my Daśarathi."
He was a beloved son to his father, a husband who acted for the welfare of ascetics,
a destroyer of those who harbor enmity, and one who always performed great deeds for the virtuous. In battle, he brought about the end of Paraśurāma’s power with his spear.
He who, as the protector of those performing sacrifices during rituals and always the fulfiller of meritorious works,
abandoned his royal status at his father’s command and retired to the forest;
[he who dwelt] in the forest that was frequented by Pitṛs and Trikoṣṭus and filled with terrifying *rakṣas* spirits.
How is it that you do not recognize Rāma, whose severed [limbs] lie there in rows,
who plays with sharp arrows, hurls great maces,
and slays his enemies?
"Having entrusted me to his brother, he has gone out to hunt like a hunter; my younger brother has been sent by me to search for him and has gone into the forest.
Then, panting, with reddened eyes and profuse beads of sweat trickling down, [he appeared].
Having revealed his inner intent, the Ten-faced One said to her:
"Now that the son of the eldest has been exiled for the sake of the son of the youngest,
who would hold Rāghava in high regard— he who resembles one who is naked and robbed?"
If he has cast out the rākṣasas— who are heroes only in their own circles— at the sacrifices of the young brahmins, O frog in the well,
what pride do you have in this?

With the enjoyments and retinues of my kingdom now diminished by my own prowess, how can it be right for me alone to say, "Hari is impoverished"? For the Lord of wealth is now devoid of Laṅkā, stripped of his pride, and robbed of the Puṣpaka chariot.
Since he dwells within my speech,
who would not know that as the cause? Like one whose boat has been shattered, Yama himself, meditating, fears me.
With a face bearing a dark hue, he sits there devoid of energy.
O Maithilī, my city is named Laṅkā, a jewel-mine located at the foot of the golden mountain that rises from the ocean.
In a dwelling sprinkled and swept, you shall be anointed and perfumed with fragrances;
wearing a large, sweet-smelling garland offered to you, dwell there together with me. Unite with the male!
"O auspicious one, I am a young man devoted to women;
Rāghava has gone abroad, that most wicked man. Abandon him, who is worth nothing at all."
"Eat and drink, O you who are intent on the work of Love; having brought the Ten-necked One under your control, rejoice in the excellent palace.
Do not be grasping, O timid one!"
“Be eager to go,
become radiant, and press against my chest.
Thinking her to be hostile, he of terrifying form desired to seize her.
Pressing his arms around her, the night-stalker seized her and plunged into the sky; as he carried her away trembling, the beasts and birds fell silent out of fear and sat still.
Hearing those piteous cries being raised loudly,
Jaṭāyu, the lord of birds, approached Rāvaṇa and spoke harsh words to him.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Prakīrṇaka-kāṇḍa.
Henceforth is the section on the commitment (*adhikāra-kāṇḍa*):
“O you who wander through the forest, do not take the lead among those who roam the woods; do not be the foremost of the lowly, but rather be my precursor. (Bhk 5.97–2)
"Fie on you, shameless one, who torments Rāma— who performs deeds that bring glory, who is renowned upon the earth as a bringer of compassion, and who carries out his father’s word—
just as the sun surely brings an end to darkness."
"O Rākṣasa,
you must lead Rāma like a servant;
[lead] this bird who causes anger among the virtuous and creates enmity for those who devour men."
To strike him, that maker of strife, the maker of sound, fell from the sky.
Beyond this, in miscellaneous verses:
shaking a canopy throughout all paths in the sky with his two wings, he—
Displaying flesh and blood, he fought with blows from his beak;
yet he neither feared nor was he ashamed.
He did not grow weary, nor was he distressed;
whether being struck or pierced, he did not turn back from the battle.

In battle, he shattered like a wretched chariot that fearsome vehicle adorned with banners, which was driven by a leader with a Piśāca face and equipped with a parasol and armor; hereafter follows the section on the sword.
He terrified the enemy and gladdened the gods as they watched;
he caused the twenty-armed enemy to relinquish Sītā.

The cool-headed Rāvaṇa, undisturbed by weapons, let out a roar; then the sky-dweller, armed with claws and beak, repeatedly tore him apart. Driven by the power of their mutual anger, the two strove to kill one another.
The rākṣasa did not flee, nor did he show mercy;
the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras waited to behold him,
while the flesh-eating bird cruelly tore away his two wings with its beak.
Seeing the best of sky-travelers cut down and rolling upon the ground, the Ten-faced one rejoiced;
mounting his excellent chariot drawn by fearsome steeds, he returned to his own city, having seized Rāma’s beloved.
The fire of desire burned day and night for the ten-faced one;
he made it known that Vaidehī was indifferent to anyone other than Rāma;
and he vigilantly kept watch over the enemy’s activities at all times.
Filled with apprehension regarding the descendant of Kakutstha, he became terrified;
yet, when threatened after making advances toward Sītā, he did not feel shame.
Furthermore, being intensely infatuated with the princess of Videha, he did not even maintain his own vigor.
"Let those who know the facts learn of Rāma's conduct," he said to his own people;
and, exerting himself, he charged the *rakṣasas* to protect Sītā.
Now, the miscellaneous verses (*prakīrṇaka*):
Rāma too, having slain Mārīca and intending to turn back,
heard the harsh howling of jackals crying out cruelly and foreboding evil;
he suspected that Vaidehī had been devoured, killed, or dead.

From afar, he beheld the brother of Śatrughna approaching; perceiving Sītā to be alone, terrified, and abandoned by the son of Sumitrā, the descendant of Kakutstha reflected: "In this time of destruction, security is difficult to find."
From here on follows the section beginning with *duh* (Bhk 6.8–9): Seeking the welfare of Sītā from the gods, he questioned Lakṣmaṇa;
the brother, overwhelmed, told him everything concerning Rāma exactly as it had happened.
Seeing that the hermitage was empty, he wandered through the forest seeking his beloved;
as if milking his own life-breath, he suppressed his grief within his heart.
"She must have gone, gathering flowers from the trees of the hermitage."
Where the ascetics are taught the Dharma by Sutīkṣṇa, there she is.
Beyond this are the miscellaneous [verses]:
"Alas! How painful!"
Bata, hī-citraṃ, hūṃ,
O Mother!
"Fie upon the gods!
O father! Where are you, O fair-browed one?"—thus he lamented greatly.
"She sat here, she slept here;
she went from here with a stumble"—
recalling Maithilī in this manner, the elder brother of Bharata grew weary.
This is her necklace for the night, this is her garland of flowers for the day;
as if pure, she hangs from the branch, withering away without it.
We have seen her repeatedly asleep, suspecting her to be dead.
To die at an improper time is a great misfortune; that we should live without her is an ill-omened jest. Do not subject me to further examination.
"O Sītā, do not hide from me; do not take pleasure in our lives. Beyond this, you have no further authority."
"I have slain the terrifying Rākṣasa of cruel prowess;
do not destroy yourself for the sake of your husband, nor fail to cling to your beloved, O dear one."
Do not see false faults; do not cause excessive distress to your food;
the left [hand] has taken refuge in the mountain.
He ran toward the river;
"Give us your voice," he cried, for our courage flowed away because of you.
You have restored our lost intellect as if it were dead, and you have sustained our life-breaths as if they were departing.
Weeping, we have opened our eyes; because of you, our mouth has become joyful.
"I shall die;
if you have no regard for me, do not fail to tell me what you intend to do."
"Lakṣmaṇa, tell me;
if she said anything that caused her anger, how can a remedy for the fault be applied if it is not known?"
"Here she anointed herself with perfumes;
here she bathed, sprinkling herself with waters;
here I called for her so that I might see her."
As he remembered this, he fell into a swoon; the fire of grief clung to his heart like a blazing flame to wood,
while the cool wind seemed to cling to him in the forest.
Yet he did not cease weeping. Bathed with water by his beloved, he wept;
likewise, overcome by grief, he poured out libations of water for his ancestors.
Likewise, even when afflicted by illness, he never abandoned his righteous duties at the proper time;
for the constant activity of the great does not falter in times of adversity.
He repeatedly summoned the heroes.
He repeatedly called out to the Rākṣasas:
"Come, you enemies of Sītā! Repel Rāghava in battle!"
"Tell me, where has she gone— she who nourished you, the fledglings of birds and the young of deer,
and who shone together with the moon?"
Rāma went to the mountain, desiring [to obtain] the daughter born of Janaka;
there, a great battle took place, which he described to Lakṣmaṇa, saying:
"O Saumitri, he was intent on killing Sītā."
The two Rākṣasas certainly fell to the ground;
this fresh blood flowed from their wounds, and this armor fell away from them.
"This chariot with its horses has been crushed to powder;
come, let us quickly descend into this mountain to search for him. I believe my anger has paralyzed me."
Despair destroyed his exertion as if by old age, and wisdom likewise withered away through grief as if by decrepitude.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa! The vulture here has been deprived of its wings;
surely this destruction has come upon it from that night-stalker who desires to devour us."
Enraged, the tiger of the Raghus blazed forth; in an instant his eyes turned red,
and he awakened the three worlds from their state of misery.
It was filled with blazing [flames] like the sun.
The supreme being of the Tathāgata was nourished as if he had accomplished his task;
the great power of that impetuous one was fully manifested.
His dejection was as if milked out, his valor was as if completely restrained,
and he was overcome by anger.
And he sighed deeply and repeatedly.
Then Rāma, possessing the prowess of an elephant, took up his bow and roared:
"I block the path of the sun!"
I split the great mountain ranges;
I drain the waters of the ocean;
I separate the gods from heaven.
In an instant, I devour the serpents in the netherworld; in an instant, I slay the night-stalkers.
Kindling my skill in weaponry, I bind Yama himself to Time.
By my own splendor, I grind the earth to powder without being harmed;
I trample upon the prosperity of the yakṣas and destroy the prowess of Indra.

“We are the messengers of King Rāma, the cutter of his enemies’ throats. We seek to recover the noble lady of that high-born king, who has been abducted by some base-born wretch.”
Thinking that the thirtieth day has passed and considering it the limit for my return, I am despondent at having failed to achieve my goal; I wait for the next world. We are dying.

"O best of birds, we shall not go to see the beloved of Kauśalyāyanī, the daughter of Kumāra, while she is still to be found," said the bird to the monkeys: "Surely you have not cultivated mindfulness."
"You should not shrink away, for this is the very time upon which you must resolve.
This is no time for those like you to be distressed from the service of your master,
just as Rāma was intensely anxious when his wife was abducted and he had fallen from his kingdom."
"Quickly make an effort to cover the southern direction;
there you shall see a golden city that covers the sky.
It is named Laṅkā, situated on the summit of a mountain, and protected by the Lord of the Rākṣasas."
Having conquered Śakra, the celestial women beheld her when she was brought down; she who,
having crushed the very domain of Indra, stood as if upon the lord of mountains—
having extracted the essence of the worlds, I suspect she alone was fashioned here upon the earth.
Without having smoothed the thousand-eyed one, and having exhausted his own skills, the Creator uttered "Enough! after much effort and fashioned her alone.
Having seized her, the wicked enemy dwelt there, having robbed the Giver of Wealth.
Having lamented that very [city] which was abandoned by Śakra, go to Laṅkā.
Having recognized your own power and desiring to seize Rāvaṇa, you who wish to question me have been told: "Do not fall asleep!"
The perfection [of your efforts] does not go toward those who do not wish to know; rather, it goes toward the man who wishes to weep.
Why have you departed like those wishing to steal, and not out of a desire to remedy your enemies?
O you who wish to know, quickly learn about Sītā!
I declare this to you:
do not consider our words to be false; act for the benefit of your master.
Advance against the enemy; gladden the best of the Raghus;
do not entertain fear.
The Ten-faced one did not accept Sītā.
Then all the monkeys, shouting "kilakila," set out swiftly toward Mahendra, the king of mountains.
And they displayed even greater fortitude. Having stayed in his delightful bower,
they cried out most joyfully and gazed upon the ocean resting upon its bed of jewels.
As if striking the mountains on its banks with waves of water in indignation,
it was radiant with full splendor as if intoxicated and rolling along;
purified by cool breezes, it stood as if woven together from rays of light.
[He saw the sun] repeatedly casting aside its waves as if they were woven together on all sides;
having deceived the sky, it remained far within itself;
and, as if thirsty, it was incessantly drinking the sweet water of the rivers.
Having shone at night with the moon, which was augmented by its rays,
it blazed repeatedly as if to conquer the vast expanse of Mount Meru.
Beholding the masses of water rising above the ocean and licking the clouds, and having reached the depths of the water, terrifying with wandering sea-monsters;
The monkeys and bulls swiftly dispatched Hanumān— the best of tree-dwellers and foremost of beasts— who possessed the great prowess of a lordly elephant and could endure coming and going.
Then, Hanumān, of massive form, leapt into the unfathomable sky.
Neither Suparṇa, nor the sun, nor the wind could surpass its speed.
At the onset of autumn, it shone like the well-risen sun;
as it moved forward, there was no place ahead that remained untraversed by it.
In the sky, the forms of Hari and the Ocean crossed paths;
they both traversed the supreme path frequented by the Sun, the Moon, and Indra.
Even the ocean could not surpass the fortitude of him as he proceeded.
Even the fierce wind could not displace that which had gone;
and as the Rākṣasī was striking him down, the Son of the Wind (Hanumān) struck her by entering her mouth and swiftly bursting through her belly.
The ocean, tossed by the wind, and the dying Rākṣasī exchanged terrifying sounds with one another; she entered the abode of sea-monsters, teeming with great crocodiles.
That Maināka mountain, which had provided sustenance for many crocodiles,
saw that he who had arisen to repay a favor to Vāyu was being protected by his father from Śakra.
Being defeated by the wind, that mountain, out of pride, said to his own son: "Rest upon me and conquer your enemy;
gather the various fruits."
Sport upon the mountain ridges;
behold the flocks of birds playing so beautifully.
O auspicious one, remain still for a moment.
Then you shall set forth again;
that task which has been undertaken by you, being skillful, shall not remain unfinished. Our joy does not rest in you alone; we ourselves abide in you.
Who would not hold you in high esteem as you rise for the sake of your friends?
Even those twice-born ones who attend upon the sun with mantras during the three junctions of the day— they too, though tormented by demons, now behold success through you.
"O Hero, attend to me without distraction;
I am a friend of the wind. While the sun shines with excessive heat, you may depart after taking breath."

“O monkey, listen! This intense heat is unbearable, as if one were being struck repeatedly from all sides by blazing firebrands. Bhk_8.16-1 saṃśṛṇuṣva kape / (Listen, O monkey!
