Associate with my auspicious groves;
now that you have arrived, my cherished desires have been fulfilled.
Who would not rejoice?
Just as Maināka is the mountain friend of Vāyu, so do I, being well-known, invite you with effort; come together and speak what is intended.
As he was lifting the mountain toward the sky, the monkey spoke to that mountain-supporter,
acting like a servant toward one who is exceedingly helpful:
“I wish to see the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) as he treats his own lawful wife as a mere mistress.”
I go with haste, O Lord of Mountains; do not harbor ill-will toward anyone.
He who carried away Sītā from the forest—he whom Hari could not overcome.
Performing miracles today, I shall destroy his power by means of my voice. Today, in the city of that wicked enemy of Raghu, I shall perform wonders;
I shall either discipline his dear life-breaths, or I shall spread my own fame.
"Or rather, advancing into the assembly of my enemies, I shall subdue their wrath," having said this,
the son of the Wind-god swiftly leaped into the sky. The Rākṣasī then began to test his prowess.
Like a comet or a star ascending toward heaven, she inspires terror.
As she strides across the waters, Hanumān enters her mouth— which spans a hundred *yojanas*— and emerges unnoticed, having become minute.
Setting out to see Sītā on the shore of the ocean,
he approached that place which was agitated by the advancing, terrible night-stalkers;
concealing his identity, he spent the day like a mere hare.

"I shall know [the way] at night," the wise one, skilled in action, vowed. Warding off many of Rāvaṇa’s followers who were aware of his presence, he entered Laṅkā at night, declaring it to be an impregnable fortress for his enemies.
He did not criticize anyone,
nor was he criticized by anyone,
even while hearing people from all sides proclaiming the virtues of Rāvaṇa.
With chatter, shouts, songs, dances, smiles, and gestures,
as if the very voice of the city were echoing before the one of purified sacrifice, Laṅkā was filled with those Brahmarākṣasas who were engaged in debate.
While the *piśācas* were thus devouring flesh and blood,
they recounted the virtues of their master in their respective gatherings;
and those intoxicated by drink, reeling on the road, went forth in throngs.
Some traveled together on vehicles such as elephants, horses, and chariots;
others offered auspicious flowers and fruits along with female attendants.
Out of anger, some would not accept the wine offered by their beloveds.
To those women who were desirous of knowing his love, he, being full of passion,
uttered a curse; he did not wish to see their dance, nor did he wish to hear the singers.
Desiring to remember Rāma, who was suffering from the pain of separation, that monkey then seemed to wish to inquire about the sight of Laṅkā; and so the moon,
whose rays dispel the darkness, rose in the eastern direction.
Desiring to hear news of Maithilī, he moved fearlessly through the palaces of the Rākṣasas while the darkness was fading away. The monkey entered the midst of a hundred thousand Rākṣasa guards.
He beheld that which even Death would die upon encountering, as terrifying; then,
when the moon was about to ascend into the midst of the sky,
the city resounded with palaces exceedingly radiant and white.
Just as one might employ the moon reflected in a drinking cup as nectar, so did the people,
devoted to the assembly, employ pleasant words;
sharpening their longing, they partook of the pure wine.
In the moonlight, a youthful host of *rākṣasa*s, their passion melting away,
drank clear wine with blue lotuses in the presence of their beloveds,
repeatedly inspiring in themselves confidence for the enjoyment of sexual union.
Those *rākṣasa*s, skilled in battle, who sought to terrify Śakra, he—
unperturbed by them— went from house to house with his monkey-skin cap.
Desiring to see Sītā, he moved about incognito and tormented the *rākṣasa*s.
He deceived the illusions of his enemies with his own illusions;
as he was thus eluding his foes, this thought occurred to him:
"The lord of the Rākṣasas is having a false proclamation made by means of spies."
Concealing his own greatness, he went to the house of Rāvaṇa— who was wandering through the assemblies of ministers and disparaging other men—
while it was crowded with celestial women illuminating the quarters of the sky.
With their supreme [beauties] drawing forth glory that is unsurpassed,
constantly exerting themselves in the acts of amorous enjoyment,
they fully understand the various playful, coquettish, and graceful movements of dalliance.
The one whose banner is the fish sits free from anxiety while having his own work done; [likewise,
women] cause the youth, deluded by intoxication, to achieve their own ends,
while they themselves bear their own beauty and worship their own bodies.
As they gazed with eyes that seemed to drink him in, he shattered their concentrated minds; Hanumān proceeded toward the Puṣpaka chariot,
which resembled the splendor of Mount Mandara.

There he beheld Rāvaṇa, who possessed the splendor of a mountain; his head and peaks resembled Mount Kailāsa, and he was adorned with trees. He appeared to surpass the beauty of the mountain itself, exuding a constant fragrance, and was seen sleeping there surrounded by his attendants.
Remembering that supreme being who, when Indra began to touch him, caused the thousand-eyed one to desist from battle out of terror,
the son of the Wind-god took a moment’s rest at the mere sight of him.
And seeing that [palace], which was as beautiful as Mount Meru with its groves shaken by the waves of the wind, the monkey desisted from his intended act;
for he saw the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) in private with his beloved.
Thinking, "Sītā is not here," the son of the Wind (Hanumān) desisted, dejected in mind.
Then he climbed the wall without waking the night-prowlers; though capable of fighting, he did not engage them, being eager for a sight of Sītā.
He reflected:
"How might I dispel the grief of Rāghava,
or how might I produce supreme joy for Vaidehī?"
"Having seen that beloved of Rāghava, I shall put the rākṣasas to flight;
for prior to seeing her, my valor would cause the destruction of the task. Thinking thus, he beheld the forest with its towering trees filling the heavens.
He saw a grove of *aśoka* trees laden with clusters of blossoms. Like a tiger among monkeys, he entered it, gently shaking the trees without frightening the birds sleeping in their branches.
In that [place], the wind blew gently, as if making the creepers dance;
the seasons, each endowed with its own excellence, did not cause distress out of fear of one another.
There, the moon was nectarous moonlight and the ponds were filled with blooming blue lotuses.

He was always made to drink [the wine] in its entirety by the command of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa). In that city, those worthy of praise were brought together, surrounded by Rākṣasa women who utterly deluded them, while they made the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) manifest.

In that [city], the enemy dwelt with Sītā solely out of passion; though he was clever and prosperous, he did not find pleasure in himself. With his gait slowing down, the monkey [Hanumān] reached the tree that was as long as a green [blade of grass].
The trees on all sides were made to rustle by the wind;
the moonstones exuded moisture, and the beds of night-lotuses shone brightly.
The clusters of blossoms, scattered by the wind,
were tossed about. Auspicious birds, warbling sweetly, hailed the monkey who was about to leap toward Sītā and whose success was imminent.
Then, through true omens that portended the sight of what was desired, Sītā perceived her future self in the presence of her husband, just as she had before.
"If news of Sītā were not to return..."
"Every effort of ours would have been in vain," Hanumān thought.
Thus ends the section on the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
[He saw] Janaka’s daughter, who was wandering from tree to tree, terrified of Rāvaṇa, and seeing no protection from her enemy, while he himself remained invisible.
Seeing her being defeated by the Ten-faced one,
he— born from the Wind, having received his message from Rāma— protected her from the demons as she vanished from them, soiled and with her hair disheveled, her smile fallen away.

The elephant-like monkey saw [the city] as if it were emanating from the sun. There, the lord of the *rākṣasas* arrived, shining brilliantly, bestowing prosperity upon those of evil views who were like demons, and boasting before the wives of others.
Though cursed and denying her, he, deluded by passion for Sītā,
offered her wealth as if he were bestowing it upon her. Longing for her, he spoke many pleasant words to her.
And being conciliatory toward Sītā, he neither became angry nor was he resentful. [He said:
"O deer-eyed one, why are you so excessively angry with me, who merely wished to see you?"
One should look upon the wives of others [with the thought]: "This is my own duty to protect.
Among those who listen, the mediocre respond; the superior do not. Others, having failed to achieve their goal, merely echo back what was said.
Those like me certainly do not [act thus].
O Lord of the World, playing with sense objects through desire and affection,
I, having been hired for your enjoyment, shall not do anything unpleasant to you.
Dwell with me in a palace;
do not inhabit the desolate forest,
and do not dwell upon the bare earth.
Lie down upon the bed, longing for love;
just as you have entered my mind without obstruction,
so do not obstruct my heart as it dwells within yours.
O you who know what must be done, do not despise the Lord of the World; for when I am seen, who would not desire the fortunate descendant of Kakutstha? Who? Ka.
He who milks a stone of milk shall obtain prosperity from Rāma;
cause Rāvaṇa to attain joy by awakening him to what is beneficial and what is harmful.
"Delighted, I shall feed you the three worlds;
why do you lament so excessively? Lay Rāvaṇa at your side."
Issue your commands to the *rakṣasas*;
do not offer up those things you hold dear.
Who would not desire to place their joined palms upon the head of Śakra?
Thus ends the section on grammatical cases (kāraka). Then Sītā, the beloved of her husband, enraged by the words of the Lord of the Rākṣasas and influenced by evil, spoke these words to Rāvaṇa.

“If you do not follow Rāma or those who are brave, then for what purpose did you carry me here by deceiving those two heroes? O lowest of night-stalkers, your conduct is not that of one who calls himself brave.”
O sinful one, since you now dwell in Laṅkā out of fear of the world-realms, reveal yourself before Rāma beholds you;
speak to the women!
"Though you follow the conduct of the virtuous, Rāma— evil in his conduct and filled with passion for another's wife— will soon shine forth here against you,
he who raised his arrows in battle as a rival to Nārāyaṇa."
"Whither will you flee, O cruel one? You have been struck down by him with his feathered arrows.
You have not spoken well, O you of fierce mind, arrogant with pride."
The All-pervading Lord will not leave even your name remaining;
though Rāma might conquer a mere tree stump, how insignificant is your capture!
O eater of men, even if you were to praise us or even if you were to revile us, what is said is the truth;
even if you were to pour [oil] into the fire, you would only increase its heat— you who are so arrogant toward me as well.
"O highly courageous one, he will bring about your destruction," having said this to the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, the princess of Mithilā fell silent. Then Rāvaṇa, of cruel form, raised his sword.
In the midst of Vaidehī, he spoke for a moment in anger, sighing deeply: "After speaking so agreeably for a long time, you have now turned away from your duty;
if you do not attend to me within a month, [I shall depart]."
“You shall die, Maithilī!”—
thus he spoke as he was returning toward the palace, dispatching terrifying rākṣasīs:
“All of you, out of respect for me, instill fear in Sītā.”
When he had departed, the Rākṣasīs gathered around the daughter of Mithilā out of malice;
for the sake of pleasing Rāvaṇa, they repeatedly spoke many cruel words.
“Sītā, you should pay homage to Rāvaṇa;
may it be well with you forever.
Otherwise, we shall surely make a meal of you this morning.”
Regarding them all as mere blades of grass, Trijaṭā spoke as they were speaking: "O you of evil conduct, destroy yourselves!
Make a meal of your own flesh."
"Today I have seen Sītā in a dream, together with the sun and the moon; she was slender-waisted, dark-complexioned, and beautiful-eyed, touching them in their midst.
Then all those women, with terrifying faces, were threatened by her as they had come.

Desirous of sleep, they went to their beds with terrifying words and deeds. When they had departed, the son of the Wind-god, having regained consciousness through Maitālī, remained for a long time hidden from the sight of the Ten-faced one.
Like one released from the bonds of debt through the departure of his enemy, he began a discourse on Rāma for the sake of awakening Maithilī.
Seeing him, Sītā thought: "For whose sake is this Rāvaṇa?"
Having descended from the tree, he approaches nearby in the form of a monkey;
appearing like someone other than his former self, he praises the son of Daśaratha.
Having arrived here without any cruelty, is it perhaps to inspire confidence in me?
If this follower of Rāghava is indeed Rāvaṇa or someone like him,
then my omens prior to dawn will bear fruit.
Living to the north of the ocean, Rāma [will reach] the city of the Rākṣasas.
How could it remain on the southern shore of the salt ocean?
Having crossed the Daṇḍaka forests to the south, as well as rivers, mountains, and forests, and even the sea, I have brought [this] to men.
"Without a fierce wind or without Vainateya (Garuḍa), no one here is able to travel; how much less so a monkey?
Having reached this state of thought with great difficulty, the monkey-lord—
Muktā was addressed by the *rākṣasa*s with but a few words: “O Mālyavatī, I am a servant of Rāma;
I am not far from Mount Vindhya, nor am I distant from Mahendra, nor am I near the ocean—I am dear to you.”

Before the Ten-necked one had arrived, I entered this forest; once he had departed, I set out to see you, O Queen, without having been noticed. Even though he was enraged as he spoke thus, I did not display my prowess.
Seeking a way to prevent the destruction of our mission, I have investigated both the higher and the lower [ranks].
Among monkeys, Sugrīva is the lord; among men, he is the friend of the sovereign.
Born as Sugrīva, the companion of Rāma, I have therefore come here as his messenger.
Having surveyed the entire city of the Lord of the Niśāṭas,
I, skilled in investigation and engaged in the work of a messenger,
beheld women who were most beautiful to behold, even among divine women.
Having encountered the most formidable beasts of prey and having driven away the Rākṣasas even more than serpents,
Rāma, eager for you and longing for union with you,
has dispatched me after he had offered the funeral oblations to his ancestors under the Maghā constellation.
"This ring is the token of Maithilī for the descendant of Kakutstha;
it was given to me by you with great affection and is held very dear.
Out of compassion for Rāma, this Lakṣmaṇa of yours is approaching."
"O King of kings, you have been brought here by a stratagem; do not be afraid.
Here, monkeys of terrifying prowess will seize Rāvaṇa;
take heart, O Vaidehī!"
Out of a desire to terrify me with his own arrogance: "When I have departed, Rāma will surely slay the rākṣasas;
by staking his very life, this Rāvaṇa has brought you here."
O best of the Raghus, he has cast aside his kinsmen and enjoyments, and has set aside his own personal excellence; for a hundred times each day, he remembers you alone.
"Maithilī, let a message be sent to your husband Śārṅga while the Rākṣasīs are still sleeping;
for she has learned of the marvel of entering the city from the monkey."
He gave Rāma the crest-jewel as a token of recognition, which was highly esteemed by him.
Having repeatedly questioned Hanumān regarding Rāma’s sleeping, eating, speaking, laughing, standing, and departing, he then dismissed him.
Displaying his supernatural powers (*abhijñāna*) and desiring to perform a terrible deed,
he reflected for a moment in his mind even as he was approaching his master:
"He who, having performed the task as commanded, does not conflict with the previous duty..."
One who performs an extraordinary task is called the supreme messenger.
Having performed a deed difficult even for others, he beheld Vaidehī.
"I shall attain fame as the one who brought news of my Lord;
this forest, which must be protected from the lord of the *rākṣasas*, has been won by me"—
having reflected thus, the monkey acted in a manner worthy of Nandana.
Announcing, "I am the messenger of those two Rāghavas; I bring welfare," I speak for the benefit of Rāma.
Who says what here? A rākṣasa:

The son of the Wind shattered the enemy’s forest—the dwelling place of doe-eyed women—where the ground was variegated by the falling of flowers, where the pollen of blossoms was tawny from being stirred up, where buds, shoots, and flowers were stilled, where birds flew up noisily from the trees as they fell, where the quarters of the sky resounded with the cries of birds, and where deer fled in agitation.
Agitated by the sound of the breaking branches and filled with the cries of flocks of birds,
they reported the night-time activities of Rāvaṇa.
That the sun bathed slowly,
where the wind blew gently, and that the snow was nourished by the heat of the sun;
The monkey speaks of the grove. Then Indrajit, the hero, overcome with rage, commanded eighty thousand *kiṅkara* demons for the destruction of the son of the Wind.
With spears, double-edged swords, iron clubs, javelins, maces, and hammers in their hands,
they spread through the quarters like those whose very glance is poison; reaching the forest,
the monkey roared as dreadfully as a thundercloud, brandishing his iron club.
Those [demons] too, with their blazing weapons, roared like clouds charged with lightning.
The Rākṣasas encountered the monkey, who was as steadfast as the ocean,
just as rivers with their surging floods meet the sea during the rainy season.
Shaking and brandishing his upraised tail, and carrying a heavy iron bar,
he stood having ascended the gateway;
he did not strike first.
The clouds of demons discharged showers of arrows upon him,
yet the mountain-like monkey neither faltered nor succumbed to fear.
The monkey shouted loudly, "Stay! and hurled his iron bar in such a way that he seized the lives of many enemies in battle.
Some vomited blood from their wounds,
others covered the earth with their bodies,
and still others, terrified of you, filled the quarters of the sky.
Their enthusiasm vanished, their bodies shattered, and their dear lives departing,
the deer were terrified by the cries of the monkey, just as they would be by the roar of a lion. Thus ends the section on *vṛddhi* after the suffix *sic*.

Those lords of the māyās, with weapons in hand, also turned their chariots back toward the monkey to slay him, for they were the ones to be slain by the son of the Wind-god. But the monkey, having taken his stand on the ground, [attacked] those who were joined together at the gateway.

Shaking his iron club, he struck down those who had gathered there seeking to seize him. Then the night-stalkers who remained after the slaughter, desiring to conceal their lives and wishing to prolong them, fled back to Rāvaṇa.
“By one [man], many heroes, though openly manifesting themselves, were turned away like those who are intoxicated,” they cried out loudly in the presence of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa).
Having perceived them to be swollen from the consumption of meat and agitated, he—
With eyes rolling in agitation, he dispatched his friends and ministers;
they departed with joyful hearts, accompanied by their sons, possessing great prowess,
uttering clear cries, and with weapons— both smooth and variegated— in their hands.
Seeing those cruel ones— extremely firm, audacious, arrived by the command of their lord, roaring piteously, with weapons raised in their hands— the monkey,
unflinching, swiftly crushed those who resembled mountain peaks as they drew near.

Having subdued his enemies, his power calmed, and filling the quarters with his roar, he— though himself undisciplined even by the Thirty-three gods— angrily and swiftly struck down those enraged ones who had arrived with haste, armed with weapons and intent on great slaughter.
As they were being struck down, the entire world in all directions experienced a heart-rending terror from the ear-piercing clamor;
their hair stood on end with fear, yet those enemies were subsequently subdued.
In an instant, their prowess exhausted by the monkey,
they were brought to ruin; having slain the Rākṣasas, Hanumān, who had subdued his enemies, proceeded once more to the Aśoka grove.
As if to cover the sky and obstruct the winds, the son of the Wind-god rose up;
yet he did not consume the forest while destroying it. May he swiftly cast away the kalpa-trees of Maithilī and grant us auspiciousness.
Trees were cast down on all sides as if to cover the earth;
desiring to conceal his own intention and wishing to quickly execute his command,
the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) ordered the monkeys— who were neither capable nor worthy of forbearance— to be slain.
He said: “May you restrain yourself; go and observe the prowess of the enemy. May you be bold in battle through your magical powers;
having been summoned, may you quickly take your stand fearlessly before the enemy in the midst of the great conflict.”
That illusory stream reached the splendor of the monkey to agitate it;
having swiftly plunged into that forest, the monkey, a destroyer of his enemies,
began to crush Akṣa, and Laṅkā was laid waste for its inhabitants.
Having extracted his life-force from the son of the Ten-faced One, he stood with a club like a tree uprooted from the forest;
he was the seeker who sought [his foe] in battle, and the endurer who endured him intensely.

The monkey struck with trees the one who wished to pierce him, the one who had been pierced, the one who was about to strike with eyes like weapons, the one who desired to play with weapons in battle,
the one who wished to play with an iron club, and the one who desired fame and glory.
Desiring to strike him again, he challenged that prince;
then, wishing to seize his banner, he fell into a swoon. Having recovered his breath in an instant, Akṣa was as if wishing to uphold the worlds with his splendor.
In his rage, he showered arrows upon the monkey, who resembled the sun; the monkey, wishing to join the quarters with his arrows and wishing to strike Akṣa with trees,
displayed his prowess in battle as if performing a magical illusion.
When they sought to overwhelm him with weapons, the monkey shone forth;
when they sought to overwhelm him with stones and trees, the monkey blazed forth—
whether desiring to make his own power known, or perhaps wishing to sustain the worlds.
While they were watching the battle, those two were dragged away by weapons;
having tormented the one whose actions were untainted with illusions for a very long time, the Rākṣasa reached the monkey on the ground and fell down, struck by an iron club.
Purified by favorable breezes and having drunk from the ocean of milk, he again broke through the forest inhabited [by the gods]; then,
raising his tail high and tossing his head, he seemed to carry it along as he moved.
Shaking its wind-tossed filaments, which were tawny like fire,
that tree fell with speed as if it had grown old; others,
having been cut down, fell helplessly as he forcibly felled the trees.
Having subdued the hosts of enemies and without tiring, he— like a lion with a mane of hair—
roamed through the forest like one unrestrained, as if about to roar after having roared.
Then, desiring to reach the further shore, he [encountered] his enemies who were returning once more.
Like a rutting elephant, he took delight in the forest of those dwelling in Laṅkā.
Saying, "If the Lord of the Rākṣasas himself had intended to fight,
I would have cut him down this very day," the monkey roamed about speaking thus.
“Upon hearing that he was slain, the Lord felt supreme joy;
and today, even as we speak, the highest delight will arise in Sītā’s heart.
Having summoned Indrajit from his presence, Rāvaṇa then spoke to him.
Like a furious lordly elephant roaming in the forest during rut, you have gone forth to the battlefields; you have brought about the end of your enemies,
and you have done so repeatedly.
"You were able to conquer the gods; you remembered your illusory powers in battle. You created weapons."
You shall see enemies who are difficult to withstand;
you yourself have struck down the weapons even of the great with your own weapons. Therefore, by my command, go and slay that evil-minded monkey.
Do not fail to brandish the *rākṣasī* illusions;
do not fail to display your prowess. Do not fail to discharge the great weapons.
"Do not flee from the enemy in battle;
do not restrain the monkey; go quickly without fear."
As Indrajit departed from the palace, he touched his feet;
having received blessings from him, he returned with the highest joy. When he had gone, the Lord of the Rākṣasas ceased his agitation.
Indrajit, skilled in valor, thinking the monkey had been conquered,
went forth desiring to cause wonder and wishing to manifest his illusory power against the enemy,
like the irresistible wind at the end of an aeon, seeking to overwhelm the world.
When the world was equal to Death (Kṛtānta) in its desire to destroy, as if a monkey in the forest wished to uproot trees or swallow his own strength,
the flocks of birds came to him in grief and seemed to weep.
Like one who has lost his kinsmen and now breathes a sigh of relief at their return,
the forest— struck by the wind of that force, its branches shaken and its clusters of blossoms shining— seemed to draw breath with a loud cry.
“O you of evil conduct, you do not live; nor do you hold power over illusions.
If you do not approach Kakutstha, [you shall perish],” the monkey spoke these words to him.
Thus ends the section on the *iḍ* [sacrifice]. Then Indrajit, together with his army, advanced in battle,
repeatedly covering him from all sides with hundreds of razor-sharp arrows and magical illusions.
Like a mountain of the Kulaparvata range, the monkey— desiring glory— forcefully scattered the nooses of the *rākṣasa*s, which were like darkness, along with their showers of weapons.
In that battle, he who bore a bow-noose was like the great sun amidst his vast mane of light.

He offered salutations preceded by the lord of the *rākṣasas*. Having manifested his strength to effect the ransom of his master, the monkey shone in battle as he struck down his enemies, having cast out all evil deeds.
Casting four wooden stakes, felling trees, and repelling enemies in battle,
he was seen wandering in many directions, obscuring the expanse of the quarters.
Striking down the fourfold hosts of his enemies who were attacking him, he overwhelmed the men of his foes.
Desiring to drive his enemies from the battlefield, he— tawny as a blazing fire,
acting as if he alone were creating light, and like one who had reached the highest limit in combat—
Śakra’s foe, wielding his bow, encountered him who bestows long life.
Shooting arrows that were like the light-makers (the suns) in brilliance,
he who brings fame struck the monkey— who himself desired fame— with his shafts.
Yet that son of the Wind-god, moving through the sky, did not place him beneath his feet.
"Though pierced in many ways by shafts that strike the vital points like masses of darkness"—this concludes the section on sentient beings.
"The horses of the vehicle, yoked to the poles of the enemy of Indra... [Bhk_9.67-1]
Having pierced their eyes, he released the Prābhañjana wind.
When they fell asleep upon the ground,
the son of Rāvaṇa then [addressed] the charioteer.
Harsh with the fear of those who had fled, he commanded others to bring [the chariot]. Desiring to praise the battle once more, wishing to instill fear,
and as if inciting his own men, he mounted his chariot.
As he was being showered with water from the trees by the monkey who acted as a rain-cloud,
Indrajit, desiring victory, again formed an invincible battle array.
Overwhelmed with rage, he seemed to be consecrating the monkey as his own successor.
With blood arising from the clash of weapons— slightly warm and dripping from wounds— he,
intending to preside over them in battle, sat before the city gate; undaunted, he held back and struck down those roaring men who were attacking.
Having endured it, the enraged Rākṣasas showered down a net of weapons that even Indra could not withstand;
yet the monkey endured it all.
With blood streaming, he struck with his iron club the leaping enemies who were reddened by the flow of blood; the monkey,
roaring like a cloud, leaped about and attacked the enemy who was rushing forward.
He bound him, who was quivering, with the unyielding noose of Brahmā. Seized by the devourers of men who were emitting sparks, he—
though capable of resisting— did not move out of reverence for Brahmā.
"Bring joy to your master;
do not fail to swiftly bring the monkey from the sky! Thus did Indrajit loudly command his own men.
"O timid one, we shall devour you once you have come here from your place, having lost the touch of our fingers," so said the enemies as they led away Māruti.
[Likewise, they spoke] regarding the twice-born in the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma.
He who protected [them] spoke thus: "This is a messenger from a human being.
He who tore off the noses of those women, as well as the maternal aunts of Rāvaṇa—
He who slew his mother’s brothers and nephews, such as Khara and others,
and before whom no demons appeared even when they gathered in terror—
this vow has come from that one born of the Kṣatriya race.
Having seen the great king fast asleep, this wicked man of malicious intent,
skilled in the art of espionage, entered the pleasure grove.
[He beheld] those whose hair was well-dressed and who possessed a luster like that of the *kapiṣṭhala* tree.
At night, he beheld the princess of Mithilā, who was established in the conduct of the twice-born,
preeminent among all women in her virtues, seated upon a grass mat like Gaviṣṭhirā,
lying upon the bare ground as spotless as the star Tārā situated in the sky.
It was exceedingly melodious among all sounds, slender, most luminous, and auspicious;
it seemed to scorch itself while transforming the forest into light—
a forest crowded with bees and rendered tawny by filaments that had become like honey.
Like a meritorious vine of gold and jewels with blossoming flowers,
shedding tears from her eyes as if pouring a continuous sprinkling of water upon her heart scorched by the fire of grief— such was she of the highest vows.

Seeing those trees obstructing him as he struck down his enemies, he angrily scattered them on all sides, like the wind itself; his prowess remained unimpeded in that great battle, for he was himself unobstructed.
The deep roar of the clouds paralyzed the weapons that had been endured [by him].
Recognizing that he was about to dry them up, the *rakṣasas*, filled with pain,
bound him with other long leather straps, chains, and the like.
Indrajit, perceiving that his bonds were being replaced by another set of bonds, became despondent, thinking:
"A divine bond cannot endure another binding, for no other fetter can overcome it. Thus ends the section on the substitution of *ṣ*.
Seizing the monkey, the Rākṣasas approached the Ten-necked one, who stood before them with his broad chest stealing away all light;
they were the fearsome Khara, Naśa, and others, whose vital organs had been pierced in many ways.
While the moon was rising in the eastern forest,
the enemies of the monkeys (the bears) said: "By him, this garden has been made devoid of mango groves and the like, yet it is not mixed with forests of *devadāru* trees."
In the forenoon, the Rākṣasas, who drink blood, approached with great joy their leader, the bearer of wrath, having seized the monkey,
the destroyer of the pride of his enemies, who was intoxicated from drinking liquor.
The enemies of the gods, who had carried away the wives of others, who were addicted to wine,
and who were prone to rivalry, bowed at his feet as they sent forth Hanumān, who humbles the minds of his foes.
"Cast down the head of the forest-clearing monkey upon the ground!
the enraged Lord of the Rākṣasas addressed his assembly,
speaking as a thundercloud roars while striking down a rain-cloud.
Then, intent upon his own welfare, Vibhīṣaṇa addressed the Lord of Rākṣasas:
"O Ten-necked One, compose yourself;
you ought to restrain your anger."
"Make this declaration:
'The messengers are being slain even though no fault exists. The Lord of the Rākṣasas spoke thus to Vibhīṣaṇa as he was leading away the enemy.
"This man is not wicked, for he did not destroy the grove of women. By him were the *rākṣasas* slain who had taken possession of my forest."

"How shall we not abandon our evil? Tell me, how can we deal with one who has previously done us harm? When my enemy intends to kill me within his own house out of anger, do not create an obstacle for him."
Know this one to be ready for departure. Those who would not slay an approaching enemy,
even though he is present, quickly bring about the loss of their rightful fortune.
Who, having committed an offense that provoked the indignation of Rāvaṇa,
would be capable— even Śakra himself— of protecting his life in this world?
That wicked one, swinging about in the depths of the forest, was merely a seeker of fruits.
He will not again disparage us by censuring our honey;
there is no further rising for Hari, nor any shining for the moon, the enemy of frost.
"There was no excessive trembling in the forest protected by me from the wind. Yet,
this monkey—
devoid of discipline and having gathered bees— has now ruined that foremost, delicious flower-essence in the forest."
When he had been thus addressed by the one with a face terrible with rage as he shook him,
the monkey spoke these conciliatory words to Rāvaṇa for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose.
Thus ends the section on the substitution of *ṇ*.
“O Lord of the three worlds, how can your anger toward one who sees a single monkey bound and brought to his house be as light as a blade of grass? (Bhk 9.110–2)
When people bow before you who have kindled the sacred fire, and when you turn your back on the desire for victory, why, O ascetic skilled in policy, do you harbor such agitation?
For there are no women who are virtuous throughout the night, nor are there any lands that are mines of jewels.
Having conquered which [enemies], these things are obtained; who would wage war for their sake? Unite with Rāma and Sugrīva for the prosperity of the world.
Like two oceans filled with jewels, [were] Himavat and Pūrvaparvata;
Rāma and Sugrīva were his friends, and the monkey troop-leaders were his servants.
Only by surrendering another's wife can these things be obtained; release Maithilī.
By restoring Sītā, you restore righteousness, wealth, and friendship with Rāma.

Granted, by dwelling in confidence and giving up Sītā, you may obtain the three [boons]. Yet, was it not made known to you by Virādha, Tāḍakā, Vālin, Kabandha, Khara, and Dūṣaṇa— nay, even by Mārīca— what kind of enemy your foe truly is?
Do not consider even the death of those who are harsh and so forth to be a cause for enmity;
for that [action] was performed to protect oneself, not out of a desire for victory.
Therefore, the cluster of his lotus-like faces trembled at the onset of the wind of his anger.
Trembling like a great lake, Rāvaṇa said to Kapi:
“What is there to say for one who has slain the Rākṣasa warriors, broken the trees of the grove,
and declares himself to be a messenger?”
It is like a messenger for you.
If the descendant of Kakutstha— who slew the hunchback, the child, the women, Kabandha, Khara, and Tāḍakā— is an ascetic, what kind of ascetic is he?
Speak, you sinner!
Knowing that pride is the fruit [of such actions], how could you have spoken of greatness?
Since it is devoid of the acquisition of jewels and the like, the conflict with Rāma was fruitless.
"The enjoyment of others' wives and the seizing of their property is indeed the very dharma of flesh-eaters;
you have declared that they possess mouths— what cause for suspicion do you have toward me?"
Speak, Hanuman! What kind of friendship exists between humans, monkeys, and rākṣasas, who are vastly divided by their supernatural powers, moral conduct, actions, and lineages?
If one is defeated by two, that defeat is not intended [as significant];
this fool has been struck down by trickery— what pride can you take even in that?

And by my command, Mārīca, intent on flight and devoid of any desire to fight, died while carrying off Rāma in the forest. Rāma truly slew the illusory deer (latā-mṛga) while it was distracted by another [prey].
Reflecting carefully, you yourself must say whether it is appropriate for great beings to kill themselves in order to protect their kinsmen by providing them with food.
"He will be forgiven by the Ten-faced One;
where is this evil-mindedness of yours?
The monkey said, "I am a messenger; there is a means for you to see him."
I deliberately brought about the destruction of the *druma* demon.
O Ten-necked One (*daśagrīva*), those who were born from you have made the world, as far as Mount Trikūṭa, devoid of moving beings.
"How do you speak thus?
'We shall not kill those of the lord of the earth.
That which was declared by you regarding the conflict with Rāma was merely the fruit of your own pride."
By that [act], hundreds of families of asuras and rākṣasas were destroyed. Since you, being weak, adopted unrighteousness as your own dharma and became fearless toward your enemy, Rāma;
This is not conducive to long-term security; just as you did not desire friendship with those divided by lineage and other such factors, so too you should avoid enmity with both men and monkeys.
If Rāma, the best among archers, slew Virādha— an obstacle to ascetic practices— having conquered him,
why was he not intended to be mentioned?
Even as he was perishing, he was unable to escape the range of your arrow;
you yourself have said that Mārīca, the great illusionist, [was slain] by the hand of Rāma. You do not remember the prowess of Vālin when he was distracted by another.
He who faints while bowing at twilight is surely oppressed by his own arms.
Abandon this war of power, which is the invention of false kinsmen; restore Sītā to him who is worthy of honor, along with your treasury, army, and territory.
When the son of the Wind (Hanumān) spoke thus in the assembly— words that were clear, harsh, and unbearable—
the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), looking around at his attendants, commanded the monkey to be burned.
Then he [the monkey], covered with bark, silk, and blankets, had his tail set ablaze and raised high.
He, whose eyes were agitated, flew up toward the sky while being gazed upon by the kings who were his enemies and by the members of the assembly.
That one, skilled in battle and honored by Rāma, waged war in the city of the foremost enemy of the gods;
and that one, honored by Bala and Haṃsa-Rāma, forcibly set the house of Rāvaṇa ablaze with fire.

The entire city was not spared by the fire with its sudden onset; yet by you, who are powerful, the calamity of the three cities was brought to an end, leading them to the mountain [Kailāsa] through the agency of women who were themselves liberated from their distress.
Having abandoned their bodies, the water-birds fly repeatedly in all directions;
the sky is filled on every side with their cries, full of melody and complete, as if it were filled with the wailing of those in distress.

There was no golden pile of dwellings that the monkey did not set ablaze with fire, nor was there any place where the melting away of snow, brought about by the intense heat, did not occur on all sides.
The *cakravāla* palindrome: The laughter has ceased, the attachment has ended;
with joy they have sported, the smiles have faded, and the influence of passion has vanished.
The women were not intoxicated, for their pride had been destroyed; what was intended for the benefit of the city was not carried out.
This is a *samudra-yamaka*.
The city of Laṅkā, with its well-kindled refuges (shrines) blazing, was consumed in its body; its lords, whose desires were not fulfilled, were utterly deprived of their sovereignty.
This is a *kāñcī-yamaka* (rhyme at the waist).
As each and every flesh-eater was torn asunder, a state of utter agitation spread;
the people, driven by fear, repeatedly performed many acts devoid of greatness.
Neither elephants nor mountain-born goddesses were beloved, nor were they cherished.
Vigata is gone away;
lalita is playful; pramadā is a woman who has lost her composure.
A great slaughter occurred from moment to moment.
The monkey did not burn that city, which had been attacked by monkeys of great and terrifying prowess, nor by men.

The lord of monkeys beheld masses of people perishing— swiftly driven together by fire, fallen upon the earth, and scorched by its lack of luster; a city that was once level on all sides and devoid of gates, yet now rendered utterly defenseless even against the most insignificant foes.
The *hārīṇyā*-*balā* plants [could not] remove the exhaustion of the women; nor did the golden ponds with their pure waters dispel the distress of the women;
nor did the trees provide relief to the women by approaching them, for their leaves and flowers were scorched by the fire.
Then he went forth fully to see Sītā in that secluded grove, where the rows of birds were agitated and the *āsana*, *bāṇa*, *kesara*, and *tamāla* trees were broken.
There, she who possessed eyes with the luster of a forest-born lotus dwelt in the woods, distinguished by her ability to leap over dense masses of great mountains.

The daughter of Janaka was seen by the deer of the trees lying upon the ground beneath the trees, according to the people’s perception; she was beloved, yet suffering and stripped of her ornaments—this is a *vipatha-yamaka*.
She, who was once so dear, now experiences great misery, fallen from her finery.

Rāma’s beloved wife was separated from him despite her pride. Your sorrow is known; you have seen the Mālyavat mountain, which possesses constant splendor and devours all worldly objects.
[This is an example of *garbha-yamaka*.
The enemy, possessing vast strength and great height, flew up into the sky without limit, as desired.
Having subdued the vast host of beings who were full of desire and pride, and having countered the terrifying army of his enemies, the lord of the gods,
together with the ocean, shone forth, transformed and all-conquering.
The agitated ocean shone along with Indra; the agitated ocean shone along with Indra; the agitated ocean shone along with Indra.

He has approached the excellent, lofty, beautiful, and foremost mountain; he has approached the renowned abode, full of courage, with eyes like lotuses, firm and established before him. He has approached the excellent, lofty, beautiful, and foremost mountain; he has approached the renowned abode, full of courage, with eyes like lotuses, firm and established before him.
The Yamaka of Beginning and End:
Wondrous, as if it were a marvel, that mountain appeared;
having encountered its speed, the monkeys were terrified and repeatedly lost their senses.
Like a lamp at the beginning [of a procession],
as he went, he scattered the waters of the ocean and shook those trees standing upon its shore.
Those Kinnaras, full of passion, occupied those flower-strewn seats that provided comfort to their limbs;
[this is] the end of the lamp.
Having quickly reached the mountain adorned with groves of trees, that vine-like monkey— having revealed his resolve for the task through a smile— decorated it with the joyful monkey armies;
[this is] the "Middle Lamp."
Although the *garuḍas*, the wind, and the sun are considered the swiftest among those that fly,
they nevertheless thought him who had returned with his purpose accomplished to be exceedingly faster than themselves.
(Metaphor)

With weapons and serpents hidden in the caves of his wounds, with the broad surface of his chest serving as a rugged mountain slope, and with the mineral pigments of blood that had flowed and coagulated, that monkey-mountain shone resplendent at that time.
There are four other varieties of this very same figure; this is a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) joined with a specific simile (*viśiṣṭopamā*).
With their moving, tawny manes like golden creepers and their rows of eyes like clusters of jewels,
many monkeys appeared like the silver peaks of a mountain at the arrival of the wind-born [Hanumān].
This is the concluding verse for this section.

The moon-like lord of monkeys, having gladdened the oceans of the monkey-hosts with his sweet appearance, spreads forth the rays of the nectar of his speech, causing the waters of their eyes to flow with overflowing joy.
(Ardharūpaka)
Having exhausted the creepers of the Vindhya mountains and drunk the waters of the pure waterfalls,
those elephant-like monkeys, at the command of the joyful Aṅgada, then shook the honey-thicket forest.
This is an ornament (*lalāmaka*) consisting of a meaningful simile (*anvarthopamā*).
Like the sun among monkeys, who dispels the darkness of despair in trees and deer, he— whose lotus-like purpose was awakened by those whose speech is dear and not improper—
having emerged from the mountain like the rising sun, entered the sky of the cave of the king’s heart, destroying the blinding darkness of delusion.
(This is an *iva-upamā*).
Hanumān went to the sky of the ascetic grove where the son of Raghu dwelt, wearing matted hair, deerskin, and bark garments, accompanied by his younger brother Nara—
who was endowed with equal tranquility, appearance, and meditative absorption— just as [the mountain] was compared to the Supreme Person (Viṣṇu) accompanied by his younger brother Nara.
Holding a jewel placed within his cupped hands, from which little light emerged as it passed through his slightly parted fingers—
resembling the moon resting upon a thin, tawny cloud— he bowed to the king with his head touching his bent knees; this is a simile.
The crest-jewel of the bride, lovely and elevated with the weight of its gems, its orb of nectar-rays fully complete, was seen together with Rāma and the hope for life;
this is a simile based on benefit (*taddhitopamā*).
He beheld him, who had come from the forest with his zeal diminished, whose body was grey with dust that had not been wiped away,
who was bereft of Maithilī, and who possessed nothing but his own dignity. (A *luptopamā* [elliptical simile]).
How could Hanumān not have been a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) that accomplished his desired aims through his own power?
At that time, both the lord of the earth (Rāma) together with Lakṣmaṇa, and the leader of the monkey host, considered him so.
This is a simile based on proximity (*samopamā*).
"O you whose minds are like the wind at the end of an aeon, what fool would grasp a cold spark and lie down in the forest of Laṅkā like a lion, merely to die as an enemy? Thus spoke Hanumān;
this is the figure of speech known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle).

Having seen here that wealth which was not seized by the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) when he encountered him in battle through his illusory power (*māyā*), and which has been made a supreme battlefield by the gods; and having seen that [wealth] which is excessively abundant, yet whose modesty is obscured by the intoxication of prosperity—*Bhk_10.36-2*... [I have come].
Or else, why does wealth acquired here on the path of the virtuous not distress anyone?
[Objection: A powerful Rākṣasa is deluded.
It is not surprising that he is angry;
for what indeed could be the reason for ignoble people to follow the path of Dharma? This is merely a rhetorical objection.
While she was dwelling there, I saw that husband of Rāmā, his anger slighted;
this is the essence of the matter I have declared to you— what is the use of further, boastful speech?

Conversely: Even if the pale and slender Sītā, through her wasting away, were to attain equality with the crescent moon, she would not surpass nor even equal the lunar digit, provided that the dark spot on the moon had not exceeded its bounds and were not yet to come into being.
"O King, strive to rescue your virtuous beloved, who has been seized by one who acts without examination, who has not served elder scholars, and who is unopposed to cruelty."
Samāsoktiḥ: That great lake, teeming with agitated beings, became parched;
it was fainting from the heat on all sides.
And water falls from a cloudless sky as desired.
This is hyperbole (atiśayokti).
Then [he saw one] whose form and dress were identical to Lakṣmaṇa’s, with his right hand extended forward as if issuing a command to depart.

The monkeys, having assembled, followed Rāma, whose respectful command had been received by the bowing Sugrīva. Then the two lords of men, mounted upon the backs of the monkeys, and the monkeys, whose eyes were tawny like blazing fire, proceeded in their respective order.
They released [the earth], they departed, they quickly came together, and they reached the ground.
The sky [sees] Mount Mahendra as a mountain—
this is *utprekṣā*.

As if to protect the earth on all sides from being overwhelmed by the surging masses of the ocean's waters, Vārtāka stands as it were in the space between the surface of the sky and the earth, having extended his body to withstand the force of the sea.
I love that mountain whose roots are established in the abode of venomous serpents, which touches the world of the gods with its hundreds of peaks,
which fills the quarters with its thick and vast slopes, and whose lovely groves are filled with trees laden with fruits and flowers.

With the humming of bees imitating the sweet voices of beloved travelers, and with the lotuses clearly mimicking the beauty of the smiles on the faces of their lovers, the lake suddenly bestows supreme delight upon the Lord of Men,
as it were full of aesthetic flavor.

The mountain, powerful and delightful to the mind, with its jeweled girdle of serpents, its broad slopes possessing unsurpassed beauty, and its dense clouds fallen like garments, seems as if it were touching the heavens with its peak-hands out of passion.
Having abandoned people who are fickle, lacking dignity, unable to bear burdens, unequal, and devoid of vigor—
just as one leaves behind a dwelling on the shore of the ocean that has become unstable— [one finds] a mountain that is firm, incomparable, lofty, and possesses clouds that are thick and towering.
This is *paryāyokti* (periphrasis).

With houses of crystal and gems, with jewel-lamps, and with the sounds of the songs of young *kiṃnaras*, it inspires the thought of the city of the gods; it is free from suffering and possesses many wish-fulfilling trees.
May he be absorbed in meditative concentration.

Then the monkey armies, together with the son of Raghu, gazed upward with expectant eyes as the son of the Wind-god pointed with his finger toward the direction— obscured by rising smoke, separated from them by the ocean, and joined by the river Sītā.
Noble!
From the mountain-cave of Mahendra, the ocean went forth, its fierce rays hidden by the mass [of clouds];
with its great waves of gathered water, it remained majestic, its shore unbreached even while capable of bearing the weight of the world.

With the light from within its vast and heavy jeweled shells, it dispels the darkness accumulated in the depths of the ocean; with its lofty and rapidly shimmering nets of diamonds, it utterly overcomes the course of the sun’s rays—
magnificent indeed!

At night, the mountain peaks of Mahendra, composed of moonstones, clearly reveal themselves to the bewildered travelers as they are embraced by the rising waters of stainless rivers that have accumulated their flow,
making the mountains appear as if they were joined together.

[He] bears the mountains and the serpents, which support the earth; they possess an unassailable splendor capable of sustaining the weight of the world, they bear many gems of great luster, and their massive bodies cause the tortoises and crocodiles to dissolve from exhaustion.
[He bears them] as if they were closely embraced.
They beheld great waves that dispelled the heat of the earth, emitting vast torrents of spray and forming rainbows with the luster of stainless jewels; like clouds with deep and resonant sounds,
they were joined with logical reasoning (hetu).
Where the mountain peaks on the shore, adorned with ornaments made of coral and gems and colored by heaps of pearls, shone as if broken by the sea-serpents;
here there is the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment).

Having filled the entire surface of the earth with its treasures, and having obscured the sky with mountain-like waves, from where could this mass of water truly exist here? Therefore, when they have come together and reached the ocean, it is merely a conventional designation for an illusion (*māyā*).
This is a specific statement (*viśeṣokti*).
Though devoid of the moon, it possesses abundant splendor; though its glory has been taken by the gods, its beauty is not lost.
Though the heavens have been churned by the gods with floods of water, it surpasses them with its unimpaired power.
This is a "disguised praise" (vyāja-stuti).
Bearing the earth, the mountains, and the remaining lords of the elephants of the quarters like a boat upon the waters,
the Great Boar— who held the distressed earth— triumphed with his strides even over that which is as heavy as a mountain;
this is a metaphorical simile (*upamā-rūpaka*).

Beholding Rāma— who was as delightful to the mind as he bore a mass of water at the edge of a river flowing over the mountains, appearing like a white silken garment (cīnapaṭṭa) fallen from the breasts of the Earth, which are the mountains—
the figure of *tulyayogitā* [is illustrated].

The ocean, though its impurities had been cast off, shone forth most brilliantly when reached by the lords of the earth— the lions among men— endowed with immeasurable and great wonders, pure, vast, and unsurpassable;
this is an illustration.
The ocean, displaying its vastness to those who behold it without calamity,
became at every moment— moment after moment— a mass of broad, renowned, and tranquil waves that never ceased;
such is the contradiction.

Though his flower-arrows were soft, he pierced him; though his breezes were cool and fickle, they burned the son of Raghu. Skilled in bringing about misfortune, that Madana caused no wound, nor did he produce a flame.

Upameyopamā (Reciprocal Simile): Then, at the end of the day, the sun and the descendant of Raghu— both possessing soft, dim luster, having reached the vicinity of the ocean, and with the world having passed away— emulated each other’s forms.
Simile and Conjunction (Sahokti):
As if stealing away all diversions from every side, the thick darkness, possessing a singular concentration fixed upon his beloved, increased along with the rise of love in the joy of the Raghus.
The moon appeared, casting away the darkness over the great ocean and providing space for the eyes to see,
as if restoring the world that had dissolved; for indeed, every great being exists solely for the sake of others.
Full of doubt:
"This is a thunderbolt; how could it come from a cloudless sky? This shower of cold arrows is unreal, for there is no wielder of the Śārṅga bow."
Thus, under the sway of passion, the son of Raghu repeatedly gazed at the moon, yet he could not determine whether it was the actual moon;
this is an example of *ananvaya* (non-comparison).
The moon shone upon the clusters of night-lotus groves where its rays were scattered, and upon the faces of the quarters— those brides whose darkness had been dispelled—
and likewise in the sky; for no other [luminary] shines as the moon does.

In the thicket where the rays of the moon were warded off by the trees, darkness— as if seeking refuge— settled like a frightened being, possessing the luster of a water-laden cloud, situated amidst the intervals of broad and uneven rocks.
Then, charming to the eye and mind, delightful like the god of love born of the heart yet of contrary nature,
the younger brother of Raghunandana spoke these words, his voice resembling the thundering of a water-laden cloud.
O enemy of the Kurus, abandon your grief for the wives of your foes, whose long hair is disheveled by their husbands’ deaths, and whose collyrium and lip-salve have been washed away by tears.
Where are you, the refuge of the worlds, and where is delusion? Alas, even one who has attained greatness in the world of men perishes utterly through negligence! (Bhk 10.72–1)
The elephant-king, with a body as large as a mountain peak, sinks into the mud along with his heavy burden; the wood does not.
What indeed is there that should be understood so skillfully?
"Even that which was not perceived by you,
or even what was done by you without prior conscious intent—
even though your own self has been won through your good deeds, your flood of affection, fearing the undesirable, nevertheless compels me to speak thus."

Having heard these words of the son of Sumitrā, Rāma, yawning and stretching his two arms as he lay drowsy, occupied a bed of young shoots with the desire to sleep, while commanding the monkeys to guard him in every direction.
Then, when the moon of dull luster had set— like a treasure-house of digits [of beauty] through the exhaustion of merit—
Joy was embraced by lotuses that took the part of enemies and friends alike, while despondency was embraced by night-lilies;
and as the moon fell from the sky after having ascended high, like Bhr̥gu,
the host of stars— possessing accumulated pure fame and bound by affection for him who had bestowed such benefit— swiftly descended after it.
Thinking, "Where are those side-long glances of yours, and where are those playful words spoken by you?
at the moment the women of Laṅkā awoke, the moon set, having mounted upon a buffalo.
Spending the three watches of the night in false sleep upon their beds, turned away from their proper course due to pride,

husbands were conciliated by their wives who were distressed at the passing of the night— even when their faults had been witnessed. [These faults] were shattered by jealousy, firmly rooted, and having cast out every branch of virtue without exception.
The trees of love for their beloveds sprouted anew, nourished by the sprinkling of tears from their eyes.
Then, fearing separation, the world— its passion renewed and its thirst unquenched— did not perceive that the recurrence of the God of Love was merely a repetition of what already existed.

When the commentary was made manifest within her heart, the eye— unable to endure even the contraction [of the pupils] produced by the pleasure arising from all the senses— stood as if powerless, conceiving itself deceived.
Seeing the slender fingers with their thin skin bent upon the broad chest of the soldier, the woman of beautiful waist [was filled with longing].
Because her mind was agitated by the frustration of her desires, she long bore malice toward her husband and even toward her own fingernails.
With her bodily movements stilled and her eyes closed, the person— whose life could only be inferred from perspiration and the bristling of hair—
became deeply embraced by her lovers once all their cleverness and eloquence had utterly vanished.
Is it darkness? Is it sleep? Is it death? Or is it happiness, or perhaps a faint?
Is this perhaps the illusion of the mind-born god?
Even as they form the perception of "what is that" and "how is it," they do not comprehend it, though they conceptualize it;
[for] the chest is covered by the breasts.
Pressing his limbs against her limbs with gentle ease,
the world, afflicted by passion, found no satisfaction; for how can satiety ever be contrary to love?

Though her slender body was limp as she was embraced and though her eyes were clearly visible, the newlywed bride withdrew them; though not being led away, she remained on the bed with a single-minded devotion solely to serving others.
At the beginning of the act of love, when she was suddenly embraced, she felt bashfulness, followed by fear and longing.
When the bride had gained his confidence, her passion became delightful through the lover’s caresses.
Then, when a certain woman was struck by her beloved with a spray of water as he turned toward conciliation,
she— her internal anger having subsided and her agitation gone— was won over solely by his prowess, even though a thrill of horripilation marked the breach between them.
Another beloved woman, though normally harsh, was touched by the rays of her lover’s moon-like face;
like a moonstone (candraśilā) suddenly gladdened, she became drenched with perspiration flowing from her agitation.
Deprived of her lord, the moon, she turned ashen, as if overcome by a swoon and devoid of all discernment.
Then, like a friend whose affection is well-known, the sweet splendor of the dawn awakened the sky. Then,

their thirst for one another not yet gone, the world— its end of night having arrived as if in an instant— went forth from its bedchambers of sleep with longing, as if constrained by sorrow and under the power of another.

One half-risen, one embraced, one submerged, one obstructed; another, desiring no further journey, having gone out under a pretext, returns again; yet another stands still, having abandoned all other tasks.
With rhythmic timing that achieves a harmonious beauty, there is a beautiful concentration fixed upon the melody of the voice.
In the royal palaces, young women sang auspicious songs in the morning, their words conveying the intended meaning.

As the sun rose, its continuous rays acting like ropes, it seemed to rescue the world— which was submerged in darkness as if in an impassable mire and whose distinct forms had vanished— from that state.

Their faces, with the redness of their lips still stained from the wine they drank, their collyrium washed away, and their radiant curls tossing about, shone forth at dawn as if they had achieved their purpose; they did not shine so before when adorned on the previous day.
Their eyes were copper-red from staying awake all night, and their eyeliner, lac-dye, and decorative leaf-patterns had vanished.

The women appeared as if exhausted by their exertions, their garments fallen away as they indulged in amorous play; though their lips were lovely, bearing a thick tint of betel and a smear of the soot from the collyrium applied to their eyes, those very lips brought dishonor to the husbands with whom they had dwelt.

She made their eyes beautiful with collyrium, her lips red with betel and full of passion, and her mouth fragrant with perfume; thus, people displayed partiality for her alone. At dawn, they discovered wounds from teeth that had been inflicted unconsciously during the time of sexual union.

Free from suspicion of any offense committed by one another, even people who were strangers became intensely impassioned; with eyes like arrows whose feathered shafts were their eyelashes drawn back to the edge of the ears, with great quivers for their hair,
wheels for their breasts and thighs, and bowstrings for their dangling earrings, these preeminent warrior-women roamed about as victors.
Seeing the breasts of women smeared with sandalwood paste and their garments freshly cleaned,

the co-wives rejoiced at dawn, their minds’ lingering resentments having subsided. In a heart afflicted by love, even that which is fickle shines, for it is captivated by its own qualities once it has found birth there.

Out of curiosity, as if peering at one another’s faces through the lattice-windows of their eyes, passion reached its ultimate height; then, when love had transcended all bounds, the world, afflicted by desire, lost its senses and failed to remember even those courtesies it had personally experienced, acting no longer with conscious deliberation.
With garments of not overly brilliant yet beautiful colors, with ointments marked by their fragrance,
and with faces lovely with contentment, the people signaled that they had attained the secret state.
Even at dawn, with their bodies anointed with sandalwood paste, they concealed their lips with their hands as they spoke.

With their glances steadily fixed, the young women most clearly revealed what ought to have been concealed. Even though the world had already been won over by mere conciliation, why was the formidable bow of their eyebrows raised?
"Tell me, is this collyrium smeared with poison, capable of destroying the eyes like an arrow?

Upon the lip that resembles a blazing fire, why has this betel-stain been applied as if it were a mere load of straw? Thus did the young women and the youths speak in their gatherings, filled with passionate emotion.
The houses shone like lakes at dawn— easy to enter, endowed with splendor, pure, dispelling distress, and vast— with the lotus-faces of awakened women.
They were adorned with beautiful flowers that had been swept, sprinkled, and honored, and with portions of fragrant substances possessing a sweet scent.
The splendor of the Nandana grove, which even the gods serve, was surpassed by his palaces filled with bees.

A bee, falling before his eyes out of longing for a blue lotus, was driven away by his hand; yet, mistaking a copper-colored lotus for a blue one, it fearlessly bit his palm, greedy for the grass-like filaments.
The bee-like Guru [the Lord] assumed a flickering of the eyes, a trembling of the hands, a knitting of the eyebrows, a heaving of the pair of breasts,
and the tinkling of ornaments, just as one does in the art of dancing. Then,
having arranged their attire so as to be favorable and endowed with the virtues of their noble lineage, the people of the city of the gods waited for the auspicious day.
At the time of awakening, he whose enemies were filled with grief set out toward the royal palace.

Like torrents of water rushing with force from the peaks of the lord of mountains, the floods of people issued from the city mansions; filling the streets like rivers, they overflowed the ocean that was the king’s court.
From the time of the awakening of the enemy of the Lord of the Thirty-three (Indra), those who were drying up— withering away from before and from above—
both the lowly and the great, attained a state of equality when they were beheld by the eyes of the men of contempt, who stood at the gate.
They were held by the forefingers of those men with heavy, trembling hands, ears, and tongues, as a mark of disdain.
The *rakṣas* stood guard with lordly elephants whose temples were covered by swarms of bees clinging to them, brought there without effort;
while the monkeys, with their forefeet smeared with the flesh from the frontal globes of rutting elephants they had severed,
and likewise others bound together by their tails, brought [the spoils] arranged in rows.
Neglected by the hosts of gods who were trembling, and cut down by the forest-dwellers who were devoid of fear,
the celestial trees were seen there scattered about, with their nets of flowers and clusters of blossoms.
He, who was intent on rejecting the elephants among the twice-born and who— out of extreme delusion— regarded all virtues as mere straw;
In former times, the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), for the sake of his own prosperity, worshipped the foremost of the Brahman-rākṣasas;
he was accompanied by deceitful masters of illusion who caused terror among people, who were seekers of gain,
and who were intent solely on the destruction of the virtuous, thereby agitating the regions of the earth where the assemblies of the righteous once stood unharmed.
It was filled with *yātudhānas* brandishing sharp weapons, crowded with *rākṣasīs* whose faces were like the bellies of wolves,
strewn with hundreds of packs of dogs, and like a forest teeming with timid does caught in a snare, it was filled with the terrified female attendants of the gods.
Like a cloud charged with lightning, he raised up a deep and resonant sound in every direction with the radiance of his abundant jewels.

He ascended a lofty golden throne, like a peak of Mount Sumeru, adorned with various jewels and highly elevated. Then his mother spoke these words to Vibhīṣaṇa, who had performed the worship of the deities, who bestowed tranquility of mind by his mere sight, and who was beautiful with his limbs adorned with ornaments.
O wise one, as you afflict the worlds,
may you— who are like a brother to those exceedingly arrogant ones— bring joy to the inhabitants of heaven; quickly effect their pacification, just as nectar counteracts poison.
One should act in such a way that she abandons the cold, her form enveloped by the mist of despondency;
though she stands upon the earth with her peaceful mass of flames spread out, she causes terror in people like a star fallen from the sky.
O joy of the family, as long as this alms-food— which terrifies the hosts of gods and is as fearsome as poison to a lion— is not swallowed by that Lord of Men, it must be consumed quickly.
Exert yourself for now!
The assemblies of Janasthāna have been struck down;
the city has been made to have its soldiers uprooted like trees and conquered.
The garments have been burned; whatever was to be done for him by his kinsman,
perform that upon him.
Before that [work] was even intended to be composed, while he was repeatedly being urged toward that purpose which brings security,
the wise one for a long time applied himself with a mind exceedingly firm and focused solely on what is virtuous, both moderately and excessively.

He went to the gate of Rāvaṇa’s palace, where the messengers of Śakra were being struck down by the doorkeepers, and where the world-protectors stood nearby with offerings; there, night-stalkers entered with apprehension and fear as trusted attendants.
From afar, bowing to the wardens and inquiring after news, he entered unannounced.
With a path cleared by respectful night-stalkers, he beheld him who was like Indra’s enemy atop a mountain peak—

seated high upon a lion-throne with a body like fire, as terrifying as a cloud at the end of an aeon, and possessing naturally sharp sparks from his eyes like a mass of smoke from the fire at the dissolution of the world.
Even with a glance given out of affection, he inspires fear like the lord of serpents;

though his form is a mass of darkness, he completely overcomes all things of renowned brilliance through his splendor. The night-stalkers, who have conquered the world of death and possess radiant luster, approached that giver of jewels.
Like the chief gods who have developed a thirst for a rain-cloud pouring forth liberated pearls, he—

having performed his prostration, with his beautiful arm resting upon the lion-throne, which was prepared by servants skilled in reading his gestures and crowded with those who had arrived before him— ascended the seat.

Then the Ten-Faced One, like an agitated serpent, with his hand adorned with gems upon blazing rings and tongues of light flickering from the luster of his many nails, extended it and addressed the assembly:
“By capable friends who have witnessed [the truth], who are hereditary in their knowledge of policy, and who are wise— ”
Together with those like you who are skilled in means, our undertakings will be successfully accomplished through wise counsel.
When the destruction of Vālin and Khara was overlooked,
and the city was burnt, [the consequences followed].
“Kṣemaka having been slain along with his servants,
and the army of our enemies desiring to cross the ocean— tell me immediately what is appropriate in this situation.”
Grasping their arms, shoulders, chests, bows, swords, maces, and tridents, the Yātudhānas—famous for their pride, led by Prahasta and others—spoke to the Ten-faced One:
"O you who consider yourself wise, having raised your staff, you have shattered Śakra, who was not even to be broken! "
O foremost among those who enjoy human sovereignty, why do you, intent on mantras, assume such gravity toward men?
Tell me, shall we grind the sun upon the earth, along with its mass of smoke and its scattering sparks?

Let the sky be below and the earth in the intermediate space; for you,
who are possessed of such fickleness, the fire has been fanned by your own tail.

“O Rākṣasas, well-supported by the king, you have spoken words worthy of your high regard; indeed, those must be uttered at the cost of one’s very life.”
In this mantra, however, wisdom is what is required, not valor.
Furthermore, even one who applies himself with diligent devotion to the practice of mantras attains the status of a Guru,
as did the man who brought Indra under his control.
Hanumān has already accomplished his task here; he destroyed all the cities.

If Agni, through negligence, burned Laṅkā while his own body was fueled by the very one who was to be slain, then reflect upon that with a divine mind: even the binding of the Brahmā-missile was a negligence.
The worlds possess immeasurable and wondrous natures,
and diverse people have conquered their pride;
therefore, apply yourselves with supreme effort toward the task at hand.
O wise ones, do not despise these words pregnant with policy!
One who desires victory should constantly observe the fluctuations— of increase, decrease, and stability—
and strive for excellence during the periods of transition and at other times.
Even the fickle Lakṣmī does not abandon him.

The prosperity of another should indeed be viewed with equanimity by one who has lost his moral conduct, whose senses are unsubdued, and who is possessed by pride and other such vices; for it is a cause for detachment [from such faults].
That which destroys [the enemy] along with its very roots at the end—

this decline, accompanied by the affection of the people and resulting in fruit, should be disregarded even by the wise king who has conquered the sixfold group of desire and the rest, provided he has entered into a treaty.

When, neither engaging in conflict nor making peace, the king perceives that growth or decline would be favorable, he should remain seated, awaiting the opportune moment; at such a time, he should not exert himself in vain.
Or, established in a state of peace, he should bring about his own prosperity or destroy the enemy through the application of secret means (*upaniṣat*).
One should cause his people to hear [of this], or having caused them to be divided by others, one should bring about a reconciliation with those who have fallen away.
Having demonstrated qualities of affection, one should cause his enemies to feel hatred and thus break up his circle of allies.
By employing such means as these, peace should be established as a method for achieving growth and attainment.
Having recognized those who are patient and cannot be incited by others, and having stationed them in fortresses surrounded by water that are difficult to overcome due to trees,
mountains, and impassable waters, a king may increase his power even when at war with an enemy. He who is unable to strike down his foes [should act thus].
Nor is he overcome by weak enemies; like a dog or a boar, he may engage in a quarrel, remaining seated while strengthening his fortresses and other defenses.
By merely setting out on a march, he should win over the enemy and proceed with his vehicle, having ensured his protection.
If one is unable to thwart the enemy and protect one's own undertakings, one should rely on another.
One should make peace with one [party] and engage in conflict with the other, or, having carefully considered it, seek advancement from both sides.
One who desires victory and understands these principles should apply them, knowing that they are beneficial to one's own essence.
By you, however, detachment has been produced in the world,
and the circle of gods headed by Indra has been provoked to anger.
But regarding Rāma, O King,
I see this to be the opposite; therefore, his adversaries are even more numerous.
