abandoned by the Buddhas. ||| Bhk_12.37-27 ||| And: "One who abandons one seeking protection from the hells is reborn in the Avīci hell. ||| Bhk_12.37-28 ||| Thus, out of fear of the Avīci hell, you should grant me your protection. ||| Bhk_12.37-29 ||| For it is said: "The wise man
At that very moment, your purpose was ruined.
That power of yours which previously consisted of a mere enclosure of walls, and which was destroyed by Khara and the others—
that power now suffers excessively from the burning of Laṅkā, the slaying of Akṣa, and the breaking of the trees.

Subdued by the six internal enemies, with deluded kinsmen and severed friends, and possessed of no virtues—O King, do not engage in a foot-fight with an elephant; instead, bow down to the Lord of the Earth, who is to be enjoyed through prostration.
Even Rāma was tormented by the abduction of his wife.
With our kinsmen, who were like ourselves, now slain,
let there be a union for us with the enemy, as heated iron joins with heated iron;
therefore, release Sītā.

O King, may the fierce heat of the protector of the earth, kindled by the violent winds of the [political] circle and sharpened by indignation, be pacified by the water of conciliation. Be gracious; let us live together with our kinsmen and servants.
O King, like two unbaked jars destined for breakage, you and I are equal in our approach to death;

yet Rāma remained steadfast in valor, full of resolve, and became a supreme and formidable enemy. Even if you consider yourself superior because of your army and your treasury, O Indra-like one, it remains so.
The destruction of the empty by the full is in vain; but when the full is broken, much is lost.
A proud man, whose self and servants are afflicted and who seeks only what is abundant, would strive even for a matter of doubt;
yet he who has already achieved his purpose does not entertain such doubt.

Surely Fortune does not bring him delight. A king who has cultivated affection [for his subjects] should undertake actions that are free from other faults, productive of great fruit, and bring them to completion.
In the opposite case, the effort would be futile.
A king who follows sound policy cannot be conquered; faults such as decay and the like are certain in conflict;
there is no fruit at all, nor is there a virtuous conclusion.
Abandon the enemy who has become enamored with the earth;
for by the destruction of your enemy,
you gain a friend for yourself.
Accompanied by his army during that time of distress for his friend, he was brought under control and made subservient;
behold, what purpose was not accomplished by the enemy’s arrow in the slaying of Vālin? The Lord of Monkeys did not approach Rāghava out of greed or fear.
He who was to be divided [from his kingdom],
though established on the path of the virtuous and having obtained sovereignty, approached him desiring to do him a favor.
[They were] those who feed on fruits, dwell in mountain cascades and groves, and are ignorant of the passion of the god of love with celestial damsels.
Those of noble birth, who are unattainable even by the best of jewels, are the foremost even among monkeys and cannot be incited by guile.
Having been consecrated in the kingdom as crown prince by King Sugrīva, who treats him no differently than his own son,
how could the son of Tārā— under the influence of Tārā herself— succumb to corruption for the sake of the Rākṣasa?

I see no one other than Rāma who is either superior to or equal to him, whom we might rely upon in times of conflict; for while the Self-Existent One (Brahmā) gave a boon [to his enemies] and thus remains regretful, Indra and the others were hostile from the very beginning.
O King, even after a long time, for an enemy who does not besiege a fortress, there is no loss—
even after ten days— such as the seizing of the rear and so forth, for those who have taken refuge in a stronghold.
O Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), this applies even to one who does not maintain the siege of the fortress.
Weapons are trees; the earth is the bearer [of them]; water is the drink; the livelihood is by means of fruits;
there are no elephants, horses, or women;
and the kingdom is not in the rear.
People are not to be protected;
tell me, what could be harmful to others?
Therefore, let there simply be reconciliation with the other.
"When examined, no other means exists;
surely, when you have been betrayed, the monkeys will soon bring all of this to ruin.
Thinking highly of what Vibhīṣaṇa had said, he raised his body, which had been bent by age.
With trembling wrinkles and a head shaking from old age, his maternal grandfather spoke thus to Rāvaṇa:
“A lone man on foot, armed with a bow, who afflicted fourteen thousand demons moving through the sky with their manifold illusions— ”
Why do you entertain the suspicion that he is merely a human being?

Surely this is a means devised by the Brahmanical sages together with the gods—tormented by the night-stalkers—to bring about their destruction; it is an invincible strategy in the world, taking the form of a man yet possessing an army of monkeys.

Just as the great Indra split the head of the Asura with gentle foam, even though his body had been shattered by the blows of thunderbolts, so too should this [work] be understood to be something of that same nature.
Where are the fingernails of a woman, capable of being endured,
and where is the chest of the Daitya, as vast as a slab from the king of mountains?
Behold this well-guided conduct of the gods.
He, in the form of a lion among men, pierced them with those [arrows].
"O you who are negligent, you who have wounded the path of Dharma and have become an enemy even to the sages— if you hold the peace of the lineage dear, O Indra among kings, then act accordingly."
Having regained consciousness by that roar, his eyes clouded with sleep yet having grasped the essence of what was heard,
Kumbhakarṇa— thundering like a rain-filled cloud in the sky— then spoke these words.
"The undertaking of the ritual action, the means,
the excellence of the person and the materials together with the place and time,
the remedy for obstacles, and the accomplishment of the purpose— they say these are the five limbs of mantra."

He who transgresses the established rules regarding the purpose, the time, the place, the ritual actions, and the means, shall not obtain the fruit of the mantra, O Lord of Night-Rangers; for one who is arrogant does not succeed when the proper moment has passed.
Even the sun, though situated in the meridian, might abandon its heat.
O Lord of Flesh-eaters, I consider the coolness of the night or the moonlight to be the root of misfortune that brings contempt from the world;
yet even so, those like me who desire spiritual accomplishment strive to speak to you with such persistence.
Indeed, those whose actions are perverse and who are mocked by others due to the darkness consisting of their own attachments perform cruel deeds and are attached to vulgar pleasures.
O King, that which was declared to be the cause for the exhaustion of merit has been practiced by you to an extreme degree; it will certainly yield an undesirable fruit. What have you not given?
"What sense objects have not been enjoyed?
Or, having overcome whom have I not stood high?
If, for my sake who has thus achieved his purpose, death should surely come for your sake, [then I shall rejoice]."
"What have you not already gained?
What is the use of these false and ill-conceived words spoken against you? By my valor, I shall maintain my composure in battle.
Having spoken thus once more while he was still asleep, Vibhīṣaṇa addressed the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
The quarters are shrouded by dust devoid of any sign,
while the winds blow distorted and turbulent; with the cries of beasts and birds lacking their natural character, they wail as if for a husband who has been struck down.
The sun, a mass of grey rays with a gaping mouth like a lion with its mane spread, rises up— terrifying to the world— to devour people as if from a hole produced by an omen.
Having set out on the path toward the peak of the Vindhya mountains inhabited by Agastya, the teacher of the Bhṛgus, the lineage of the Bhrigus, has departed.
The priest of Śakra is seen during the day,
and meteors fall, shaking the earth;
they cry out with cruel voices, like flesh-hungry rākṣasas longing for the slain.

Carnivorous beasts with mouths like blazing fires roam fearlessly all around our city; even though the cows have udders as large as jars, the cowherds milk them only slowly, and the milk is discolored and tasteless.
Furthermore, when the sacrificial fire is well-kindled, it does not blaze, for insects and hair have appeared within the oblations.
Therefore, O Rāvaṇa, out of affection for me, you should perform a service in return while I am speaking;
for those established in the conduct of a servant say that even what is painful is beneficial in the long run when it pertains to one’s position.

“Before the enemy can satisfy his hunger for human flesh with those who are crushed, mangled, ruined, shattered, trampled, terrified, pierced by cold weapons, or hacked to pieces— before he does so— he must first bow down to him. Furrowing his brow and casting aside his composure, he becomes terrifying with eyes that are fearsome and harsh.
The exalted enemy of Śakra, manifesting his own power, uttered these words of formidable import:
“A stone shall float upon the water, but a leaf shall not;
darkness shall flow away from the sun.”
Fire is the enemy of the moon;
I am a supreme victor in battle. O grandson of Pulastya, consider these things equal:
one who is being defeated, one who is unappeased amidst prosperities, one who harbors secret enmity, and one who displays malice even at the time of receiving honor.

May our lineage not possess diverse occupations, dispositions, or speech; may we not have [excessive] kin or clothing. On this earth, relatives do not constantly desire the prosperity of one of equal status even at their own expense.

They bow down to their enemies and do not tolerate the prosperity of their kinsmen with hearts burning with envy. Today, through your excessive joy at the conquest of Laṅkā, your wicked inner self has been revealed to an extreme degree.
"Shame on you! Your mind is falsely directed toward me. Speaking thus, he struck him with his heel.
Then, suppressing his anger through forbearance, he said:
One should subdue anger with fortitude, pride with humility,
delusion with wisdom, and incapacity through the power of enthusiasm.
He rose up together with his four ministers and said to that lord of the night-rangers: "May you be well, O Great King;
remain here without me."

When a foolish patient does not eat wholesome food because it is bitter, and thus remains afflicted by disease, the fault lies with the physician; it is clear that the patient harbors resentment when being told what is beneficial.
Devoid of solitude and proud of himself, the master is gratified by things pleasant to the ear though unwholesome; alas, this is a great misfortune for his friends! (Bhk 12.83–2)
Just as someone who lives in constant danger, playing with a snake that has entered his house, lives only by chance; even so, if a fool lives while serving a king,
that alone is his gain.
"You have dealt this blow with your foot because of your own faults, striking me as I stand upon the path of Dharma.
"That must be considered together with your chief ministers: which of us two brings about infamy?
Speaking these words repeatedly and forcefully to the lord of the night-stalkers, who possessed many virtues—
Fearless, he emerged from the city of his enemy to pay homage at the feet of the Lord of Men, which were praised by his foes.
Then, having learned through the words of the Son of the Wind that he had arrived and was known for his virtuous conduct, the King— whose heart was as heavy as a mountain—
delighted him with the hands of the lords of his own city, using collections of water.
At the edge of the shore, the night has faded— charming with pleasant breezes, playful with the rays of the deer-marked moon, and having bound Rāma in a state of delusion.
A terrible battle was joined by Rāma at the onset of day against the one dwelling in the salt waters.
In that flickering [bow], the essence of impetuous fury was like the solar disc risen high;
while upon the great arrow— produced by the enemy, accompanied by smoke and water, and possessing a deeply heavy shaft—
the earth with its mountains and the assembly of serpents were mounted in doubt regarding Rāma, the upholder of the world.

Avoiding with fear the salt waters that are the abode of turbulent waves, fierce water-elephants, and vast, treacherous mud; waters filled with formidable, excellent serpents whose hoods swell with fruit-like venom; and a mass of water radiant with the movement of great snakes.
The salt-water ocean has reached the shore, where the caves are agitated by the arrival of Hari’s army;
where herds of deer roam among the swaying trees, and the dwellings of women are adorned with many clusters of flowers;
where there are groves of trees with golden shoots, and the excellent, lofty, flourishing trees cast a cool shade.
The excellent protection [is provided] by the mass of water that restrains and wards off the mountain ranges and the circle of the earth;
the earth is supported by the force of the restless waters, which is free from contact with the high waves.
This is a *kulaka* consisting of these seven mixed verses.
Then, having prostrated, the Lord of Waters, his arms resting upon the Gaṅgā, spoke these beneficial words for the future to Rāma, whose complexion was as dark as a thick, green tamāla tree;
the first half [of the speech] was irreproachable.
The lofty bodies of the best of mountains,
the water that has no source, the wind that carries away flavors—
The multitude of sunbeams is not cold;
for you, Māyā is the supreme cause of saṃsāra,
arising from exertion and appearing as red.

Withdraw your arrow, which possesses a luster like that of the destroyer of the cold (the sun); gather your mass of water back into your ancient and beautiful abode. [That place] where the movement of Hari is difficult to find, whose base is water, and whose expanse is blocked by thick mud.
"Tell me, what is easy to traverse when devoid of water—that which is terrifying with whales, conchs, crocodiles, and elephants?

To go to the shore of Laṅkā, let the monkeys cross with ease by means of a great bridge built over the waters; let those who can endure the weight of mountains carry the mountain ranges, their bodies heavy with the burden."

May Rāma’s arrows sever the multitude of enemies’ throats— which have been obstructed by the cessation of their laughter— at the onset of this great battle, even though I am bound within deep waters by a massive mountain.
And may those with lovely smiles depart, having severed the connection to fear through the intense bond of the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*).

To slay the one with many arms and great strength, and the lion-elephant whose body was like the peak of a mountain, these six [monkeys] rushed forward suddenly. These were the miscellaneous [verses].
When the son of Daśaratha resolved to depart, the vast army of monkeys gathered together with the desire to go.
The first half-verse is irreproachable: [the army] whose minds are like a Buddha’s ocean, agitated by the onset of seizing the mountains;
the strength of Rāma, capable of bearing the seizure of the best of heavy mountains, tawny with the fire of destruction.
Suddenly ascending into the sky, it reached the depths of the pure waters of Varuṇa’s abode;
it plunged into a network of mountains where the movement of the gods was obstructed by lofty, massive cliffs;
it was terrifying with the fearless, wild dances of lions, and its cavernous waters were rich with the sweet fragrance of elephants.
With clusters of flowers swaying amidst swarms of bees, with water-lilies and flocks of intoxicated *kurara* and *kāraṇḍava* ducks;
with terrifying caves teeming with serpents, and fragments of the earth’s surface covered by the tusks of elephants;
its many beautiful waters are pure, captivating with the cries of cranes and tawny with the pollen of lotuses.
[He beheld] the Great Boar, who was like a mass of snow meeting the sun-gem, whose thick smoke from the celestial trees was produced by their union;

who was filled with the deep and passionate roar of men accompanied by elephants agitated by the sound of Hari; and who possessed massive, powerful tusks smeared with the mud from his snout’s contact [with the earth].
Then, hosts of monkeys uprooted these five mountains, which were entwined with one another and embraced by their arms; from them,
the remaining peaks— with their summits clearly visible— scattered the clusters of sunbeams and stars.
All was faultless: [the mountains],
well-supported by lofty great peaks, with their rugged ridges held fast by their arms, desiring to bind the salt waters in many ways, ascended into the vast expanse of the sky.
With many white clouds and the luster of a great stainless iron sword for its body,
it is like the snowy mountain with its rows of birds bound to it, filled with the cries of intoxicated ospreys;
crowded with beautiful swans and filled with the clamor of cranes moving about fiercely.
Carrying the fragrance of flower-pollen and water, its expanse purified by contact with the waters of the *samaya* scriptures,
those deer-like trees, suddenly burdened by the weight of the mountain at the onset of the binding of the salt-water ocean,
ascended the mountain on the shore where the movement of the enemy was halted by the arrival of Rāma and filled with fear.
These four [mountains] were joined together;
then they were properly placed by the son of Agni at the head of a troop of monkeys, and those mountains,
with their unshakable peaks and ridges, plunged into the great ocean.
By him, who was ineffable and faultless,
the ocean of milk increased, becoming the source of [the gods'] senses.
Rāma was gratified,
the lord of monkeys rejoiced, and the enemy there trembled with fear.
Suvela was seen,
the water's edge was reached, and the monkeys rejoiced.
They wandered about, leaped, and danced, performing what was called the "single-interval" [dance], which is irreproachable.
They feasted,
they sang,
they leaped up together, and they sat down.
They clapped their hands, raised a great shout, trembled, and rejoiced.
They departed; they came together.
*Ākhyātamālā* 13.29–30: [He who has] a body as beautiful as a mountain of clay, and whose fragrance is made sweet by the scent of *kakkola*, cloves, and *badhā*.

The salt water, with its many broad waves rising high upon its shores, was restless as it approached the banks; yet, in the sky, that vast and pure mass was bound by the mountain range, which— capable of bearing the weight of the celestial Gaṅgā— held back the salt waters within its excellent enclosure.
And the army of Rāma ascended Suvela, that best of mountains with its network of peaks made beautiful by the binding of rows of trees;
it was terrifying to the heart of Rāvaṇa, with its tawny and flickering manes, and it filled the deep,
vast hollows and caves of the forest thickets with the tumultuous roar of the inhabitants of Laṅkā.
It possesses the great shade of *tamāla* trees crowded with hosts of gods engaged in the enjoyment of the sound of lute music;
it has a dense shade formed by *kesara*, *hintāla*, and many sap-filled sprouts;
and it holds the essence of the passion of elephants, provoked by the fragrance-bearing wind carrying the scent of Airāvaṇa’s rut.
A forest where the network of tender, golden, and shimmering sprouts grows in the shade of lofty trees;
a grove of swaying pomegranate trees whose hue is like a flowering forest that strikes fear into deer;
resounding with the cries of sweet-throated cuckoos; and filled with great *sāla* trees crowded by massive trunks of water.
It possesses a lattice of jewels bound with trembling sprouts that seems to drip with drops of water;
it has a mass of rays from lofty gems and a deep resonance produced by the clashing of mountain waters;
it contains the assembly halls of beautiful cave openings and is like the city of the gods, filled with the joyful cries of immortals and *cāraṇas*.
With a great, stainless jewel for its chisel and a wall reddened by the stain of vermilion;
with the night-dwellers’ desire to roam obstructed by the fear of the encounter between the heroic lion and the elephant;
containing a terrifying cave with great serpents, and resounding with the tumultuous, vast, and dreadful cries of many birds.
The great *sāla* forest, crowded with herds of elephants, boars, lions, bulls, and deer;
where the moving sprouts display their grace; where the earth is tawny with the pollen of lovely lotuses;
and where the young creepers of the clove trees provide a magnificent smile amidst the flower-stalked arrows.
With its pure jewel-like gold peaks, it obstructs the passage of deer through the mud by means of its lofty, great walls;
like Mount Meru with its surrounding slopes ascended by the immortals, it possesses the *mandāra* trees whose sap is turbid with nectar.
With its excellent trees burdened by fruit and moving slowly, it bears charming flower-garlands grown nearby.
With caves profoundly deep due to the weight of abundant water originating from the moonstone (*hariṇa-kalaṅka-maṇi*),

its body consisting of mountain clefts beautiful and white with liquid gold, crowded with water-elephants (*jala-kāma-dantin*) and filled with the shimmering rays of lion-jewels (*hari-maṇi*) licked by herds of deer whose coats have the hue of a cluster of sprouts.
Capable of enduring fierce winds, it possesses the splendor of a mass of towering clouds with terrifying roars,
and the beauty of mountain ranges embraced by rows of white water-bearing clouds.
It is full of vitality, bound by the salt waters of the ocean, and its physical exertion is stilled by the abundance of fruits from the trees.
The army of Rāma, eager for battle, mounted upon elephants, gateways,

and horses; the enemy force was fully armored, enduring the fatigue of war, with the terrifying sound of heavy *paṇavas*, flutes, *guñjās*, kettledrums (*bherīs*), large drums (*pelorus*), and cymbals (*jhallarīs*), along with the tumultuous din of *ḍhakkās* and bells.

[He saw] a chariot with a formidable bow fixed upon it, its thick body concealed by a stainless iron net; possessing the quality of a beautiful, broad frame formed by the collision of restless horses and elephants;
and [armed] with swords, javelins, spears, great battle-axes, excellent crescent-headed arrows, and heavy, massive maces.

At the commencement of the battle, those hosts of monkeys, adorned with the heroic sentiment and ornaments, accompanied by their swift-moving horses and elephants, and causing the earth to tremble, were impetuously obstructed by Rāma;
they were agitated and longed to shatter the mountains surrounding Laṅkā with their steady roar.

[This pair of verses describes: The formidable army of monkeys, dwelling in the waters, on the banks, beneath excellent tall trees, in mountain caves, and in the hollows of groves; agitated by the mass of rays from the fiercely blazing sun; possessing a shadow like a multitude of water-bearing clouds heavy with the weight of rain—[this army was like] the host of Rāvaṇa, in order to be understood [as such].
He ascended the watchtowers, trees, couches, palaces, archways, garlands, and assembly halls.
Then the Ten-faced one, his soul overwhelmed by passion and having revealed his enemy’s power through his spies,
bewildered Sītā with a phantom Rāma and dispatched his army to do battle.
They blew the conchs, struck the kettledrums with their sticks,
and filled the flutes.
Guñjā berries jingled when struck by hands;
ḍhakkā drums were sounded, and paṇava drums resounded when beaten.
The *kāhalā* trumpets were filled [with air],
the *pūrṇa* drums resounded,
and the *mṛdaṅga* drums beat steadily.
As the bells of his own chariot were struck, they tinkled for a long time, and the kettledrums resounded loudly.
The horses neighed out of joy,
the elephants trumpeted deeply,
and the terrified young camels bleated.
The ranks of infantry cried out; the horses, terrified, reared up;
and the bulls bellowed most violently.
The noble women were agitated, they grew faint, they fainted, and they grieved for their husbands; they roared and they rejoiced.
The heroes shone, were praised by their enemies,
bound on finger-guards, struck down their foes, and went forth in retreat.
They strung their bows, mounted upon chariots and other vehicles,
drew forth flaming swords, and brandished heavy maces.
They whirled their spears,
took up auspicious arrows,
wandered about, and cried out.
The foot soldiers leaped up and ran about; they were struck by lashes of whips and dragged along by the pulling of reins.
The horses galloped away; [the riders], devoted to liberation, cast off their own heavy burdens with ease.
To the elephants they gave their quivers; they spread their blankets all around.
They tightened their waistbands and raised high their banners with uplifted crests;
they sought to reassure one another and embraced their women.
Those who cherished their sons struck them on the head and kissed them;
the elephants, perceiving the profound [intent], seized [the riders] unharmed,
and their rut increased and shone forth.
And he leaped up with joy. The deer moved clockwise around him, and the jackals howled auspiciously.
With his left limbs he quivered, and his mental states became serene.
By the command of Rāvaṇa, Prahasta exerted himself with great vigor.
Mahāpārśva and Mahodara entered the southern gate;
Indrajit advanced toward the west, while Virūpākṣa himself went to the north.
Virūpākṣa desired to occupy the eastern quarter along with [Mahodara].
Rāma heard all of that,
set out with his army,
drew his bow, and then fastened his quiver.
Then he looked toward the son of Sumitrā and gave leave to his forces; he paid homage to the gods and cast off his bed of leaves.
They shone forth and rose up.
The monkeys roared, pervaded the quarters, and leaped upon the mountains.
Then they shattered the trees,
and the earth split open.
The sky rained down blood as red as a cow’s footprint; deer fled toward the left,
and birds shrieked inauspiciously.
Blazing torches were seen,
jackals howled inauspiciously,
and the earth trembled.
Rāma suspected the arrival of something inauspicious.
Having heard that his enemies, the Rākṣasas, had approached, Rāvaṇa,
stationed upon the top of the rampart, personally prepared himself for battle.
The Rākṣasas discharged arrows,
hurled spears and sharp-edged missiles,
brandished swords, and dragged him with their outstretched nooses.
They pierced him with sharp javelins and likewise with various lances;
they crushed him with maces and cut him apart with whetted discuses.
The monkeys struck him with their fists and likewise bit him with their teeth;
they hurled lofty mountains and shattered trees as well.
They rolled them about with their tails and brought them to destruction with their palms.
With their nails they tore [each other], and in their rage they violently crushed one another upon the ground;
headless trunks (kabandhas) came into being.
They said, "The warriors have crossed the rivers of blood;
their lotus-faces shine with banners as if with foam."
The elephants sank in the blood-mud; the chariots did not advance, and the horses also became submerged.
The soldiers did not dare to advance.
Each city gate was blocked by ten million upon ten million enemies,
and thirty-six crores of monkeys surrounded the lord of the monkeys.
His body became emaciated,
trembling,
and exhausted.
They cried out, they rolled about, wounded, and they fainted.
Vavamu vomited blood,
and both groups of soldiers were parched with thirst;
meanwhile, Prajaṅgha fought with Sampāti.
Struck by that tree,
he trembled, cried out intensely, and perished, losing his life.
In battle, Nala gouged out the throbbing, burning eyes of Uccaiḥśravas;
Jambumālin, struck by the son of the Wind with a stone, gave up his life;
and Vibhīṣaṇa crushed the limbs of Mitrighna with his mace.
Sugrīva struck Praghasa with his fist,
and Rāma pierced many others. The head of Vajramuṣṭi, struck by Mainda, was severed.
Nīla cut off Nikumbha’s throbbing head with his discus;
Virūpākṣa was deprived of life, struck by the arrows of Saumitri; and Dvivida released his life-breaths, [struck] by the brilliance of the thunderbolt.
The mace, having been hurled by the conqueror of enemies, was received by the son of Vālin;
then Aṅgada crushed his chariot along with its horses using a tree.
Seeing that deed of Vāliputra, the entire world was struck with wonder;
all the *rākṣasas* were terrified,
and Rāghava held him in high esteem.
Sugrīva rejoiced;
the gods, filled with wonder, exclaimed, "Excellent!";
and Vibhīṣaṇa offered praise.
The monkeys praised him;
indeed, it was wonderful that Lakṣmaṇa rose up and Rāvaṇa’s son vanished.
Then Rāma discharged his arrows;
the enemies were terrified,
and being pierced, they let out terrible cries.
The flesh-eaters devoured the slain;
the blood of the wounded dripped; and the severed arms moved for a moment.
Even when their heroic faces were cut off, he of firm wrath did not abandon them;
the rest fled away,
while those who prided themselves on being heroes felt ashamed.
Rāghava showed no mercy, and none among them maintained their composure;
they perished like moths in the fire, and the heroes cried out, "Alas! Alas!"
When the sun had vanished and night had taken its place,
that night-like darkness devoured both the monkeys and the rākṣasas.
Indrajit became exceedingly fierce and summoned the serpent-missile (*sarpāstra*);
he, having become invisible, summoned the enemy host and laughed. He then afflicted the entire army.
And he restrained him with arrows; he discharged shafts,
which reached him like [the coils of] a serpent.
He instructed them regarding the army and summoned the two descendants of Raghu;
he then said, "Even Indra could not defeat my illusion, so what need be said of mere men?"
And when they were informed once more by those serpents regarding the two descendants of Raghu,

When he has met his death, by whom will his enemies be slain? When I am intoxicated and struck down by my foes in battle, what happiness shall I behold?
For who, other than one maddened by war, would attack his enemies in combat?
The performer of a hundred sacrifices (Indra), free from hesitation, will challenge me as he prepares for battle; and when Nikumbha is slain, his purpose will be accomplished,
and Hara’s satisfaction will be fulfilled.
"Laṅkā will be destroyed,
O Devāntaka!
Abandoned by you, I shall fall under the power of the enemy."
"I shall die, or I shall be victorious; even if my sons are slain,"
"I shall swiftly destroy my enemies;
I will not live on in suffering.
"The sages will smile," [he thought].
The gods will say incessantly:
"The family of the Rākṣasas has been destroyed by the evil policy of the Ten-necked one.
O Father, who could have imagined that Rāghava would [confront] Kumbhakarṇa?
In battle he will cut his limbs and tear his vital organs;
the sun will fall upon the earth,
and the earth will tremble.
The wind will be shattered; the sky will be struck with fists.
Indra’s moon will flow like water, and the ocean will overflow its shores.
Water shall burn, and the masses of darkness will vanish before the hot-rayed sun;
Kumbhakarṇa, enraged in battle, shall be overcome by a man.
These things have never been imagined by anyone among people. When Kumbhakarṇa has been slain, the monkeys will ascend Laṅkā and devour the rākṣasas.
Arrogant, they will destroy my hermitages;
filled with joy, they will mock the young and the old and dance about.
Without that chief of the *rākṣasas*, who else would restrain them?
My indignation is supreme:
Rāghava will desire Sītā.
What happiness indeed will he obtain from that loss of his kingdom?
"I shall kill Vaidehī; I shall have her devoured by the rākṣasas."
Or I shall bury it in the ground as the cause of its destruction;
I will not pursue the prosperity of the world, nor will I strive to live.
I shall find no delight in sense objects, nor in an empty dwelling, nor in my kinsmen. With whom shall I rejoice? In whose happiness shall I rejoice?
And who shall rejoice in my happiness?
O Kumbhakarṇa, for what purpose are these enjoyments to be accepted if they are without you?
Those riches which will come to me when my friends have perished— will those not be calamities in times of misfortune, their enjoyment marred by grief?
"The city will soon perish;
the monkeys will arrive quickly;
you have no intention of making peace"—this was the eloquent speech of Vibhīṣaṇa.
"We shall not speak, for we have been provided with wealth by the king;
we shall fight," this was what Prahasta spoke.
"A human being named Patkāṣī shall fight in battle against the king of the man-eaters, who is difficult to conquer even with divine weapons and chariots.
Or else, I shall arm myself to fight."
I shall not wear armor like one who is devoid of courage;
today the flesh-eaters will thirst for me, and the earth shall drink the blood of my enemies.
I shall draw forth my fame;
I shall remove my enemies through action;
today, Maithilī will experience grief due to the loss of her husband.
The lord of yakṣas will feel remorse,
and Yama will not rejoice; moreover, the female monkeys in the forest, who have neither husbands nor sons, will grow weary.
The *rākṣasas* will sleep peacefully and wander about without fear;
the *rākṣasīs* will not shriek.
And they will joyfully devour men.
"Before this very moment, at dawn, I shall certainly become happy;
then, in the time that follows, there will be another, a second moment."
"In that place I shall go to conquer the Lord of the Thirty-three along with the immortals;
thereafter, free from envy, I shall return once more to Laṅkā. To him who spoke thus, the foolish Indrajit approached.
“Saying, ‘I shall desire to fight,’ you who strike fear into your enemies— O Great King, you possess no higher knowledge (abhijñā).
We two shall conquer that which is protected by Śakra.”
"O you who are filled with the qualities of proud gods, we two shall go together to the abode of the gods; you do not possess the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*),
for we shall forcibly destroy Yama along with the lord of the yakṣas."
And we two shall bring back the jewels and reach this city.
I shall look upon my enemies once more.
You shall not grieve, O Rāvaṇa;
you shall see the world devoid of Rāma and you shall traverse the quarters. Together with your servants, you shall instill fear even in the abode of the gods.
Today the Lord of Gods will bow to you; he will offer you his salutation. From you, the sages shall arise, and you shall preside over your adversaries.
Today in battle, I shall know all those who pride themselves on their heroism;
and today, I shall be known by the hosts of enemies who consider themselves brave.
Today, I shall cover the earth with the severed limbs of the forest-dwellers.
"I shall mount [the chariot] that resounds with a sound as firm as the clashing of masses of clouds at the end of an eon, and which shines with the luster of raised banners, bows, and swords.
Today you shall hear the carnivorous beasts crying out, their faces terrifyingly red with blood, satiated in battle where enemies are scattered, mangled, turned away, and destroyed.
Then, desiring peace, he offered oblations into the fires.
The warriors recited the Vedas and performed auspicious rites;
they honored their elders and protected the children.
The women raised her with tears; likewise, they assigned her duties and clothed her.
They smeared themselves with it and then ate meat and liquor;
they drank honey-wine and mādhvīka, and partook of whatever foods they desired.
They brandished their beloved weapons, donned their armor,
and undertook solemn sacrifices.
And likewise, they cursed their enemies;
they worshipped the Four-faced One (Brahmā),
honored the Brahmins, and offered praise to them.
Śakra’s enemy smeared himself [with unguents], and he desired an excellent vehicle.
He put on armor rich with jewels and fastened a brilliant sword;
he mounted a formidable chariot.
Then, beating drums of great sound and blowing auspicious conchs, they proceeded ahead.
They beat the mṛdaṅga drums and filled the lutes with their melodies;
the bards offered hymns of praise.
Proclaiming words to one another, they let out lion’s roars and terrified the horses and elephants.
Seeing no other signs, the solar disc did not shine clearly; clouds rained down blood, and unbearable winds blew.
The black antelopes turned left;
the soldiers forgot their weapons;
and the horses and elephants spat blood, becoming exhausted and distressed.

Not counting them all, he rushed upon his enemies; with sharp swords he severed his foes, and likewise pierced them with javelins. He cut them down with the edges of discuses and struck them firmly with spears.
They pierced [the enemy] with fierce-tipped arrows and tore them apart thoroughly with javelins.
The monkeys, leaping about, violently shook the trees along with the mountains; they struck with their fists out of rage and bit with their teeth as well.
They struck swiftly with their knees, and they wounded [him] with their palms and elbows;
they hurled various weapons released by enemies.
Śakrajit trampled the foes and whirled them about on all sides.
And from the road, [there arose] a most terrible [sound],
which caused everyone to tremble; yet no one knew him as he was joining [the path].
They did not perceive him bearing his bow, nor did they notice him discharging arrows; yet the enemies knew they were slain by him.
Not hearing any sound from one direction, fleeing from another, crying out for help in yet another, they were struck down by others still.
They rolled about, were torn asunder, and blood flowed from them on all sides.
They labored in exhaustion, were not satiated, and having been wounded by him, they died.
Distressed by this, Lakṣmaṇa was about to invoke the Brahmāstra for the destruction of all the rākṣasas,
but the joy of the Raghus restrained him.
Then Indrajit, having gone into the sky and slaying the illusory Sītā with his sword, became invisible;
the son of the Wind-god spoke these words to him.
"O Rākṣasa, let this Sītā not commit any offense; she has not strayed from her husband's side. O wicked one, do not seize her while she is so distressed!"
"Śakrajit said, 'One must do what causes pain to one's friends,' and drawing his sword, he cut off her head. For whose sake we have waged war against our enemies— "
Saying, "We shall cross the ocean," the son of the Wind-god approached Rāma. Thereupon, the two heroic scions of Raghu were overcome with fainting and likewise cried out.
And as they were crying out hotly, long and loudly, the descendant of Pulastya spoke to them both: "Do not weep;
surely that wicked man has gone to Nikumbhilā after deluding us."
"Do not remain there; staying there, you would be slain by us, like an oblation in the fire,
while the fierce Brahmāśiras weapon and the chariot have not yet been acquired."
"Brahmā ordained his death before that deed was completed.
Rāghava gave his command to the son of Sumitrā and to the leaders of the hosts;
they, along with Vibhīṣaṇa, accepted it with great joy.
They approached Nikumbhilā and were hemmed in by the rākṣasas;
there, the two armies waged a great slaughter against one another under the command of the guardians of the directions.
Having swiftly conquered these *rakṣasas*, Paulastya and Lakṣmaṇa beheld Indrajit there, established in his abode and composed in meditation.
He was offering oblations into the fire while reciting the supreme mantra.
Brahmā, the conqueror of Śakra,
did not move from his meditative absorption.
Then Saumitri challenged him and let out a terrifying roar.
There Indrajit became agitated and spoke these words to his uncle:
"You were born here..."
In this world you nourished your body with wine and meat; in this world you lived, yet how is it that you have begun such a cruel act right here?
Did you not see your own hand [stained with blood]?
You did not disregard your kinsmen; O sinful one, you did not tremble at unrighteous acts,
nor were you afraid of worldly rumors.
Defamation of the Dharma:
"Surely you have neither known nor heard this."
“Having cast aside his kinsmen, he will undoubtedly attain lightness.
Then Śakrajit was addressed by his paternal uncle with these words:
“Do not transgress falsely!”
"May you not bind me with the conduct of a fish;
I was born truly into a lineage of sinful rākṣasas,
yet such conduct as that was never born within me."
Just like your father.
While being restrained by me from faults that lead to ruin, Daśagrīva took no pleasure [in them]; therefore, I abandoned him.
But he should not harbor enmity; nor should he acquire the property of others,
nor touch the wives of others.
He constantly sought to seize the gods,
was negligent toward the welfare of the virtuous, suspected his friends and kinsmen, and held his elders in great contempt.
By those very same faults that I abandoned my father, he was left by me;
therefore, he became angry and cursed me with twenty-two [rebirths].
With twenty-five arrows, the son of Rāvaṇa struck his kinsman and the king;
he then destroyed the four horses of that Saumitri.
With arrows he cut through the ocean’s current and likewise shattered the chariot;
then the son of Rāvaṇa showered Saumitri with arrows on all sides. As they both brandished their spears, they struck one another.
They both repeatedly discharged arrows. Lakṣmaṇa hurled the Vāruṇa weapon, while Indrajit hurled the Raudra weapon.
Having encountered one another, those two weapons were destroyed.
Then the Rākṣasa unleashed a terrible weapon of the Asuras;
from it fell a great mass of stones, spikes, sacrificial posts, and mallets.
Laksmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, paralyzed that most difficult-to-conquer array with a weapon of Maheśvara.
Then Lakṣmaṇa called to mind the Māhendra weapon, endowed with fierce power;
by that terrible [weapon] he arrived and carried off the head of the enemy.
All the immortals were satisfied,
the leaders of the monkey hosts rejoiced,
and they embraced the son of Sumitrā.
And Rāghava smelled her on the crown of her head.
The army of Rākṣasas wept, and the lord of men wept;
he cursed Maithilī and, overcome with agitation, set out to kill her.
"This is improper," said others; those who were authoritative restrained him, and his kinsmen blocked his path, shrouding him in grief.
Yet his heroism expanded, and his indignation also grew.
Then Rāvaṇa’s entire army prepared for battle; they worshipped the fires and paid homage to Śaṅkara.
To please the twice-born and for the sake of peace, the *yātudhānas* were struck with fear.
A wind, delightful to the mind and fragrant with ghee, blew from all sides; and the auspicious sound of "May there be merit" (*puṇyāha*) and "May there be well-being" (*svasti*) was heard rising up.
The warriors, for the sake of peace, bore upon their heads water free from blood;
they offered jewels and cattle, and then they invoked blessings.
They smeared themselves with pure white sandalwood paste,
arrayed themselves in variegated garments, and wore beautiful garlands.
Others quickly donned their armor;
they sharpened their weapons and polished their collections of swords.
Mounting their elephants and other mounts,
they set out with great haste;
the sound produced by that army filled the sky.

The quarters of space were filled with the tumultuous sounds of musical instruments. At the gates, there was a great throng of chariots, horses, elephants, and demons; and it was accompanied by terrifying, portentous omens.
The monkeys were terrified; they shattered great trees, swiftly uprooted mountains, and seized massive boulders.
Then a battle ensued, as the monkeys and rākṣasas struck one another.
They overpowered one another and could not endure the crushing conflict;
the dust of the earth increased.
It pervaded the ten directions and dispelled the distinction between "other" and "one's own" for the monkeys and the rākṣasas.
Then, in that darkness, the rākṣasas felt enmity toward both their own kin and others.
Even though they were monkeys, they were merciless toward other monkeys; being utterly cruel, they bit them so fiercely that blood began to flow,
and from that blood, a mire was formed all around.
Deep rivers flowed,
lakes were formed,
and that thick dust was laid to rest.
And his enemies were thoroughly subdued.
Then Rāma, shaking his great bow, was amazed at the torrent of weapons; for neither his own [instruments] nor those of others acted without being directed by him.
They saw [the enemy] cut and pierced on all sides by Rāma’s arrows;
they heard the cries of "Alas! Woe! but could not discern Rāma himself.
He shattered the hosts of enemies and crushed their horses and elephants.
He crushed the array of chariots, yet his movement remained unknown. There were ten thousand elephants and great-souled chariot-warriors.
Fourteen thousand well-bred horses and two hundred thousand foot soldiers were led by Rāghava, the wielder of the bow,
to their destruction during the eighth part of the day.
He wove together what seemed like the realm of Yama; he created what was like the playground of Rudra; and with the slain great rākṣasas, he covered the earth as if with mountains.
The gods and gandharvas offered praise; the monkeys were filled with wonder; and joy expanded within the lord of monkeys.
The descendant of Pulastya considered it a marvel.
The Rākṣasa women wept aloud and reviled Rāvaṇa.
The people, including both the young and the old, were bewildered,
and the rest of the folk cried out in battle;
they obtained safety from all sides, yet Rāvaṇa did not desire it from men.
And they said, "This is the fruit of that harsh speech resulting from his repeated practice.
Thereupon Rāvaṇa, mounting a most terrible chariot, rushed forward,
and the earth trembled.
Terrifying vultures swooped down;
clouds accompanied by lightning rained down blood that soaked his garments;
and fearsome winds blew from the sky.
The jackals howled inauspiciously; disregarding those ill omens as they circled about, he brandished his bow in battle and overwhelmed his enemies with a flood of arrows.
Then Sugrīva’s arrows destroyed the enemy kings; thereafter, the surface of the earth resounded, grew weary, and was seen [in distress],
with blood dripping from it.
Stained with blood and exceedingly distressed,
the army of flesh-eaters, oppressed by Sugrīva, fell into ruin. Then Virūpākṣa sported in the battle with a rutting elephant.
The lord of monkeys crushed his head with his fist;
immediately thereafter, he pulverized Yūpākṣa with a boulder.
Enraged, Aṅgada struck Mahodara soundly with his fist.
Then the ten-necked one, enraged at the destruction of the forest-dwellers,
deprived the *rakṣasas* of their protection and scattered his enemies in all directions.
He gazed upon the descendant of Kakutstha and dared not attack him.
He twanged his terrible bow and struck fear into his formidable enemies;
he leaped toward Lakṣmaṇa with arrows and swiftly overtook him.

Jiṣṇu rushed toward Rāma and assailed him with showers of arrows. Unperturbed, Rāma warded off that rain of shafts with his own broad-headed arrows (bhalla) and struck the Ten-necked One in return with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
As they traversed various mandalas and encountered unceasing volleys of weapons,
those two caused the world to marvel,
yet the heroes did not falter.
They pierced the sky with their arrows, struck the earth with those that had fallen, swiftly struck one another, and repeatedly displayed their martial skills.
The Rākṣasa of cruel prowess took up a divine weapon and unleashed great serpents as well as terrifying tigers and lions;
then Rāma restrained that [attack] with the fire-weapon (*pāvakāstra*).
He played a fierce and most terrible [instrument], whereupon mallets and other such things fell from it;
then the lord of the earth silenced it with the *gāndharva* [science].
Then Narāśaṇa pierced Rāma in all his vital spots with sharp,
feathered arrows; thereafter, Lakṣmaṇa shattered Triśiras’s banner.
Vibhīṣaṇa quickly struck the charioteer and pierced him with many arrows;
he stunned the horses and swiftly shattered the chariot.
The Rākṣasa was not shaken;
he instead raised his heavy spear against his brother.
As it came flying toward him, the son of Sumitrā cut it into three pieces with his stone-tipped arrows.
Seeing them making no sound, the night-stalker became enraged;
raising a massive great spear equipped with eight bells,
he struck the younger brother of Rāma with it.
He, deprived of life, took refuge in the earth; Rāghava’s arrows became incessant,
and he was tormented by them.
Then the Ten-necked one swiftly left no survivors upon the field of battle.
The elder brother [of Lakṣmaṇa] drew forth the quivering spear from the son of Sumitrā and sprinkled those medicinal herbs which had been brought by Hanumān.

The brother born of Sumitrā, having come to life, embraced that long-bodied one; he smelled his head and asked if he was free from ailment. Then they all exerted themselves and rushed toward the enemies to fight.
And Rāvaṇa was reached by another chariot without difficulty.
Mātali said, "A battle on the ground is not equal to one for one standing in a chariot," and at the command of Maghavat, he brought forth that most formidable chariot equipped with weapons.
That [missile] was mastered by Rāma;
then the ten-faced one discharged the *pāśupata* weapon.
The king conquered him with the Śakra-weapon;
then Rāma, with a hundred thousand arrows, overwhelmed the night-stalker and destroyed his excellent steeds.
And he urged the charioteer to go quickly.
Inauspicious omens were seen,
and the circle of the earth trembled.
Rāvaṇa hurled a trident, and the lord of the earth hurled the spear of Indra.
Having met one another, those two attained a state of mutual stillness.
Enraged, the Rākṣasa pierced Rāma’s chest with a hundred thousand feathered arrows;
Rāma then struck back even more profusely with his shafts, while Rāvaṇa did not grow weary.
His charioteer destroyed the chariot. The Rākṣasa threatened the charioteer and again brought forward his own chariot; both discharged arrows and both pierced the two draft animals.
Both cut down the enemy's banners, yet neither of them wavered; both blazed with courage and both applied their skill with precision.
Both displayed their illusory powers;
both heroes did not grow weary,
and both swiftly traversed various mandalas.
And yet neither of them could be perceived,
as both charioteers struck their two chariots together, and the two radiant horses collided.
Then, in the battle, the Rākṣasa extended from his illusory head a hundred [other heads];
of these, one hundred were severed by Rāma with his feathered arrows. The oceans were thoroughly agitated.
The mountains trembled;
Śakra was seized with terror,
and he swayed.
The earth trembled. Then, for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, Mātali recalled the fierce weapon that the Self-Existent One had fashioned for the lord of the earth.
In whose arrows there is the wind,
in their fruit the sun and fire,
and whose weight is like Mount Meru;
His body was subtle and composed of space. Resplendent with Garuḍa feathers, that abode of all splendors is remembered as having struck down the most terrible Rāvaṇa, felling him to the earth.
As he bound on his monkey-faces with great composure,
the assembly of gods praised the king who had conquered his enemies;
for others, the ends of the quarters were free from all agitation.
The descendant of Pulastya, having lost his kinsmen,
experienced grief; then the sorrow arising from their connection to him overwhelmed Vibhīṣaṇa, and he wept loudly for the Ten-faced one.
"The Ten-necked one, though accustomed to a costly couch, now lies upon the ground; agitated, he does not look at me,
nor does he grant me an answer."
"O Ten-Necked One, this ripening of karma has been seen by me regarding the future.
You were told that [this] was for your own benefit; why do you not restrain your anger?"
Calamities quickly befall and prosperity swiftly passes away those who,
out of pride, do not abide by the doctrine of the proponents of reason.
Out of greed, their dependents prescribe what is unwholesome for their long-term future.
Prosperities do not come to one who listens to what is pleasing from them. The wise and radiant ones see correctly and speak correctly.
O Great King, those who are thus despised become exhausted and desist. He who constantly consumes even bitter things that are wholesome, like medicine, [attains health].
For that purpose, he serves the learned and never desponds;
pride arises in everyone.
A man becomes negligent regarding his own welfare and indulges in what is unwholesome for his growth, by which he perishes;
he generally feels aversion toward virtues.
He feels no affection for anyone; he bears enmity even toward the great; though possessing growth, he withers away.
By what means do I find consolation?
How do I breathe, fallen into misfortune, when my brother, the lord of the three worlds, sleeps upon the earth? Alas! Fate remains awake even amidst such hardships.
Shattered by that force, my kinsmen roll upon the ground, they wither away, and they lie sleeping;
jackals tear at their flesh.
The earth drinks the blood;
birds devour the flesh of those who share a kinship with the Ten-necked one.
He who once stood at the head of the great battle against Pūtakratu—
By chance, even that Indrajit’s head was pecked by crows;
Svarbhānu, having finished his daily rites, spat out the sun he had swallowed;
and no one seized by Rāma ever regains their prosperity again.
O King, not knowing this, you boasted of your own prowess;
you were unwilling to give up Sītā,
and you did not master the objects of the senses.
If ignorant people ever speak thus regarding mantras,
you even approve of them;
how indeed can you not understand what is for your own welfare in that matter?
"O descendant of Pulastya, when you were not asked, your maternal grandfather spoke to you for your benefit in the mantra, saying, 'I shall not do it,' and then,
out of delusion, you replied."
"Do you know, O Great King,
what Vibhīṣaṇa said?
That long ago, having been insulted in the assembly, he would have abandoned me in his anger."
In the sacrifices, this Madhavan [Indra] eats the oblation without fear;
the wind blows at its own will, and the sun rises. The Yakṣas rule over riches.
Yama subdues the rākṣasas;
Varuṇa extends his noose; the moon now rises;
and the collection of seasons comes to rest.
The forest-dwellers perform austerities;
they do not pay homage to their kinsmen,
nor do they serve the immortals.
Fortune is being stripped away in Laṅkā,
and prosperities are fading;
he does not know this.
For him there is no reversal when you have died.
Śakra embraces his power,
and Hari protects his fortune.
Worshipped by the gods, they rejoice, marvel, and experience the dawning of dense clouds [of merit].
Bearing their weapons, those gods, filled with indignation, desire battle;
they shine forth and likewise remain watchful for the openings of those who eat flesh.
They roam about all around Laṅkā and even surpass us; they manifest their own power and diminish our fame.
The arrogant ones spread through all directions and abandon the state established by you; the base ones crush us and mock you as you fall into misfortune.
The winds, repeatedly bringing tranquility, purify the world on all sides;
O Great King,
you have already attained peace— how much more so now?
Grief envelops my mind;
yet my being seems to become tranquil, and light wipes away my suffering.
I release my vigor; without you, with whom shall I commune? There is no kinsman more affectionate than you.
I cry out in the void.
How shall I cover [the fire] arising from my wrath?
Bereft of you, my kinsman, I weep for myself as one who is protectorless; I cannot measure the extent of your benefactions.
Now Śakra and the lord of the yakṣas are neither terrified nor impoverished;
they have not abandoned their pride and remain arrogant.
O Ten-faced One, we are not being afflicted;
even though we are deprived of you, we still carry out our duties and maintain the will to live.
Fie on craving, which destroys what has been done! I would burn my own body if you do not grant me your word;
for your virtues, when remembered, only prolong my grief.
"Who, laughing, takes off my own garland and decks me with it? Who brings me near to a seat?
For who speaks pleasant words to me?"
I shall not go to Laṅkā as long as I still have life remaining;
when will joy come to me if I do not see you?
"I shall die within a moment, overwhelmed and with my kinsmen wounded;
I have spoken what is beneficial to you, O Mantra, and I do nothing that is displeasing to you."
The women of the inner apartments and the citizens, deeply distressed upon hearing that he had been slain by Rāma in battle,
rushed toward him and tore out their hair.
They cried out in extreme distress,
repeatedly reciting the benefactions of their lord and lamenting with great sorrow; the citizens bowed down to Rāvaṇa and wept with tears.
Then Rāma spoke these words to the agitated descendant of Pulastya:

“O Ten-faced one, why do you grieve for him who is a donor, who stands upon the heads of his enemies, who performs sacrifices, who gratifies his ancestors, and who remains undefeated and unharmed in battle?”
No delusion arises in those such as you during times of calamity;
do you not see that all these people depend upon you?
“You ought to perform the funeral rites for your brother and dispel the grief of these people;
for if you, the leader, have perished, O Lord of Night-Rangers, the burden of the kingdom will sink unborne.”
Then, free from resentment, Paulastya spoke these words to Rāma:
“Even one who is not to be pitied, when setting toward his destruction, might cause distress to his kinsmen.
May the gods ordain that for us, so that we may [die] as Rāvaṇa did.”
May we conquer our rivals and may we prevail in battle. And may [the deeds] be performed by the Ten-faced One, as they have been by no other in our lineage.
Even when gods, men, and hosts of enemies are turned upside down,
only such a friend as you, who is capable, can sustain one's life during such a calamity involving kinsmen and provide consolation.
If you were not my refuge, I would surely die within a moment;
for this is our hope.
"O Lord, may we live under you, O Ten-headed One!
How could we find pleasure in that land which is censurable,
where there is not even the birth of a full brother for one twenty cubits tall?"
Then Vibhīṣaṇa addressed those bowing ministers:
"Go quickly to Laṅkā and enter the royal palace."
"O you who are highly worthy, take up those magnificent robes with haste;
raise aloft the excellent banners and carry forth the finest sandalwood."
One should release incense into the sky, weave beautiful garlands,
and bring immeasurable wood, camphor, agallochum, and saffron.
The sacrificial vessels might be carried away, the fire might be extinguished,
and the clarified butter might be consumed by the officiating priests.
One should prepare sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass;
one should quickly bathe [the image] with bathing powders and smear it with beautiful pigments.
One should adorn the ten-faced Rāvaṇa with jewels worthy of him;
one should clothe the lord of the Rākṣasas in two pure, fine garments.
The officiating priest, having placed a garland upon him, should set him down upon a deer-skin with his head facing east.
One should pile the sacrificial vessels upon the clan-heaps according to the rule,
offer the oblation into the fire, and the chanters of the Sāmaveda should sing the Sāman hymns.
Then, having gone to the city of Laṅkā and performed everything exactly as instructed, they stood near the final oblation and, with tears in their eyes, spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa:
“Everything has been done exactly as directed.”
O Great King, you should strive together with all your kinsmen to perform the fire and water rites.
Like one who knows, you should not fail to exert yourself; you should maintain unwavering steadfastness and remain firm in the affairs of your kinsmen.
The darkness born of grief is to be abandoned. This is not to be conceived: that even you should grow weary amidst hardships.
A wise person should never be deluded like an ordinary worldling.
And wherever you may dwell, there shall be no other Rāvaṇa.
Whatever you might fall into in such a situation is greatly condemned.
It is a marvel that we should speak to you of what is beneficial in this regard.
Moreover, even your direct disciples [have said]: "O Indra’s priest, you must abandon your negligence during times of distress;
O Lord of the Nairṛtas, people desire that you should abandon negligence.
Or else, [if you do not,] your enemies will lament over your downfall.
How much more so your kinsmen!
If you were to protect all people properly like a brother,
and if you were not to become utterly deluded, then the night-stalkers would find relief.
Then he went to perform the fire and water rites for his brother. Having completed what was to be done, Rāma then spoke these words to the rākṣasa:
"With a golden pitcher, the one possessed of meditative concentration sprinkles the waters upon the head."
"O Vibhīṣaṇa, you are the king of the Rākṣasas; look upon Laṅkā!
You should properly appease those who are angry, and win over those who are greedy with wealth."
O descendant of Pulastya, you should honor those who are proud at the proper time, and you should console those who are terrified.
This is my supreme wish.
How could you not rejoice like the enemy of Vṛtra?
For everyone desires a friend who is established in prosperity, since [he is] a friend;
may you prosper among your own kin.
May you slay the hosts of enemies;
may you be honored by the virtuous; may you remain steadfast in their stability.
You shall be worthy of the affection of your friends; you shall be saluted by the denizens of heaven, and you shall drink the Soma.
O King, you must ascertain those actions that are to be abandoned— namely, violent deeds that cause harm— and you must carry out the duties of the city-dwellers in accordance with the Dharma,
acting with affection.
Always present among all people,
may you suppress anger and maintain uplifted pride.
May you be seen by the *rakṣas* demons, and may they be seen by you as well. O King, let the wrath of the young and the old toward those who have slain the soldiers be extinguished.
May those of noble intellect, well-versed in the scriptures, attend your assemblies;
may you take delight in the path traversed by the divine sages, which abounds in dharma;
and may you perceive the designs of your enemies through the eyes of sound policy.
Then, having approached Sītā, the son of the Wind-god said: "By good fortune you are prospering, O Vaidehī;
the thorn of the three worlds has been slain."
"Grant me permission; let me slay these low-minded female Rākṣasīs who guard you. Take away your attachment for them."
O Thirst, you whose intentions and actions are terrible due to your wicked conduct—
let your intellect become murderous; act with cruelty toward these [beings].
"O Queen, we shall do this last favor for you.
Then Sītā, with a compassionate heart, spoke to the monkey:
"May he be appeased."
Their intellect is directed toward those small beings who provide a morsel of food;
this is a fault by which he has been struck down.
"Indeed, it is not my intention that you should commit the terrible act of killing a servant;
rather, become my instrument for this task and go speak to the descendant of Raghu.
'O Rāma, I wish to see Maithilī!'"
"Behold you without delay.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," he went and said to Rāghava:
"O delighter of the Kakutstha lineage, let the Queen be brought here, for she is eager."
Having drawn a line on the ground and heaved a sigh, and having looked at Vibhīṣaṇa with a frown, Rāghava said, “Bring Sītā here, adorned.
Having gone and bowed, she was addressed by him with these sweet words: “O Maithilī...”
"Abandon your grief, O Vaidehī;
set your mind on joy. Abandon your hatred toward Rāvaṇa."
Abandon the grove of women!
Bathe, anoint yourself, fumigate,
put on your garments, and fasten a garland.
Put on jewels; offer oblations into the blazing fire;
and consume the five products of the cow.
Cut through the darkness born of obstruction;
ascend the golden palanquin;
destroy the desires of your enemies.
"Let the lord of the kings consume the grief arising from separation from you;
therefore, from this moment forth, you shall remain occupied with your own household duties.
Together with Rāma, undergo the initiation for the horse-sacrifice with all haste."
"Be seen by your husband with affection; look upon Rāghava with love.
This is the command of your husband;
no hesitation should be made in this matter."
Adorn your body;
if it is the right measure,
strive to go to Rāma.
O Goddess, unite with Kakutstha in joy,
attain prosperity yourself,
and ascend to the higher realms within a moment.
O Raghava,
within a moment from now,
O dear one, you shall become the mistress of the earth.
Instruct the people of the city who are under the command of the king’s wife. Arise, O lady, in accordance with your husband’s will, and strive likewise in your adornment.
"And remain there to behold that lord of the earth who is worthy of being seen.
Having carried out the command exactly as instructed, the daughter of Janaka ascended the vehicle, her face veiled with fine silk cloth.
Bowed down with shame, overwhelmed by the memory of the suffering of separation,
and shedding tears, she went before her husband and wailed piteously.
Then the king, having become suspicious of her conduct, said to her:
"I desire this: 'O Sītā, I do not take you; depart from here.
For you, having been embraced upon Rāvaṇa’s lap, have carved a line upon my heart."
Fix your mind on Sugrīva, or seize the lord of the Rākṣasas;
enjoy the pleasures from Bharata.
Either choose Lakṣmaṇa, or go according to your desire;
let the hopes centered on Rāma be abandoned.
Where is the renowned lineage of Raghu,
and where are you, who have dwelt in another's house?
Give your heart to someone else!
We do not exert ourselves for what is undesired. Go as you please, O Vaidehī;
may your paths be auspicious.
"Let your desires for others be appeased; abandon the suspicion directed toward me.
Then the princess of Mithilā, of noble lineage, spoke these words to the king:
"Let the suspicion born of my being merely a woman be relinquished regarding me."
"O descendant of Kakutstha, fear fate; likewise, feel shame before the people for having falsely provoked me, who am helpless and have been carried off by an enemy."
My mind’s activity is fixed upon you;
my body has been seized by a demon.
May the upright gods take full cognizance of these true words.
O Wind,
purifying, purifying the three worlds as you move through the bodies of living beings, know that my intellect has become deranged.
O Waters, you who roam the earth as the most purifying *khamaṭas* and *dyāmaṭas*,
understand my virtuous mental activity.
"O Vasundharā, you who support the worlds by constantly holding them up,
know my conduct to be unswerving day and night.
Withdraw your fluids."
Shine forth, destroy the darkness,
and roam through the sky!
Thus, O Sun, who possesses sharp rays,
strive to understand my conduct here; may you abide in heaven.
Dwell upon the earth,
remain in the abode of serpents; O Ākāśa, dwelling thus, [be for me].
Awaken to what has been done and what remains to be done;
prepare the funeral pyre, O son of Sumitrā,
for this is the remedy for this calamity.
"Either may Rāma be pleased with me today, or may the fire consume my sins,
as I ascend the funeral pyre prepared according to the will of Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa."
Having seen [him] and circumambulated him, she spoke these words to Rāma:
"I am casting my body into the fire; I have been suspected by you.
Let all of you, including the monkeys, know and hear this."
O Fire, burn me, who am wicked, with your blazing body;
or else, protect me, who am wounded and stained, as a friend would.
I am she who has reached you according to the ritual, like a stream of clarified butter poured into the sacrificial fire at the rites, reaching you whose garland of flames is raised high.
Then, having lifted her up, the fire said to Rāma regarding Maithilī:
"O descendant of Kakutstha,
how could you have suspected your virtuous beloved?"
O Rāghava, this purity would not have existed if I had abandoned it; yet I did not abandon it, for I have no partiality toward anything other than the Dharma.
Furthermore, had that evil-minded enemy not sought Sītā there, had he not spoken cruelly at any time, nor ever boasted of his own prosperity,
and had this pure-minded woman not formed an attachment for him there—
Out of intolerance for the truth, you would have become like Rāma, [obsessed] with Sītā. If you had lived with her for a long time, would you not have seen her character?
Or would you not have observed her actions over the course of much time?
If this darkness were not to be laughed at, it would remain to be grieved over for as long as one lives; even the sun would have fallen [to earth], and this earth would have been shaken.
O King of kings,
had there been no such fickle behavior toward women here, the guardians of the world would have come to this place; thus, these [beings] would not have been harmed by the Kali age.
It is truly marvelous that you would have acted so harshly toward a woman;
had she perished out of fear, what fruit would you have obtained? For if that woman, though free from fault, had died there out of terror...
In a world devoted to envy, the basis for speaking of that [envy] is false. Just as you would not have been resentful, so too your father,
King Daśaratha, would not have come in person seated upon his celestial chariot.
If Maithilī, devoted to her husband, had been enjoyed by another, Śiva— the wielder of the trident whose mount is the bull— would not have remained present there as a pillar;
for how could he, the lotus of the gods, having arrived, have brought you joy?
O Indra among kings!
When the world-hero Dhātṛ was wounded in his character by Sītā,
he then bowed down and was addressed by Brahmā as the sovereign lord of kings.
“Maithilī would not have been sorrowful in this world, had you not practiced this;
we would not have harbored doubt, had you not placed it here.”

Or rather, what is so extraordinary about this that it would have been right for you to do it? If your activities had proceeded according to reality as it truly is, [then this would not be surprising].
"Since you were instructing the world, Rāma would have descended even more [into the world] than that. Then Śaṅkara said to Rāma, who was about to depart:
"Did you not realize that Nārāyaṇa is the unborn Self?"

O Great King, who else here would have taken away the lives of the arrogant enemies of the gods, or who else would have exerted himself in deeds for the benefit of all people in the destruction of the Daityas?

And even in that place where you might have failed, why did you not bring your desired purpose to completion? By propitiating his father with the Kaikeyī [boon], he brought great suffering upon Bharata.
Rāma beheld the thousand-eyed Indra, desiring to pay him homage.
Then, by the boon of Śakra, the hungry monkeys were restored to life;
they became like trees laden with fruit, bending low and radiant with luster.

With trees of fragrant flowers teeming with swarms of bees, and lofty peaks turned tawny by the pollen of young *madhūka* blossoms; with waterfalls cascading through the crevices between its rocky ridges—that Mount Suvela spread forth the splendor of its luscious fruits.
With forest edges bending low under the weight of abundant fruit, stirred by breezes carrying floral pollen, it stood there.
The joy arising from the slaughter of their enemies was nourished by the monkeys through the dripping masses of honey;

the tree creepers, laden with their own fruit, were bent low and covered with swarms of bees; and those fragrant plants, growing upon the surface of the earth and easily plucked, did not fail to remove the exhaustion of those who enjoyed them.
Then Rāma, with a joyful heart, said to Hanumān:
"O monkey, tomorrow you shall set out for Ayodhyā,
which is protected by Bharata."
You shall again find footing in the sky amidst rows of bursting masses of clouds;
you shall behold the spray of the cool water from the lord of waters.
O monkey, you shall enjoy [them].
O Mahendra, you possess the plateaus of the mountain where the moonlight-born lilies bloom together with the natural radiance of the sun that has transcended its path,
and which are covered by sandalwood trees, having cast away the weariness of the cold.
You have shown those beautiful slopes of the Malaya mountains;
yet the slender, delicate creepers on the Vindhya hills, adorned with clusters of blossoms and swarming with hordes of honey-bees, will not allow you to proceed.
Filled with joy, you will soon behold Kiṣkindhā, frequented by your friends; remembering your former sports there again and again, you will look upon it with partiality.
You shall be shown by you the Mālyavat and Daṇḍaka forests.
I, who for a long time have been tormented by the pairs of opposites,
have reached these two delightful hermitages of Sutīkṣṇa and Śarabhaṅga, which were once frequented by Hari and are now filled with deer, sacred waters, and birds.
"You have passed beyond the delightful grove of asceticism, which is nothing but suffering;
out of curiosity, you shall stay on the sacred and variegated Citrakūṭa mountain.
After that, the sage Bharadvāja will be shown to you by you."
And the people who behold her have their sins washed away by the waters of the Yamunā.
Having flowed and flowed from heaven, having leaped upon the head of Śambhu and descended to the earth,
you shall then plunge into the Gaṅgā, who is like the very embodiment of merit in liquid form.

From the edge of the forest, you will perceive many pleasure-trees for the city folk, possessing a luster like great blue stones, situated on the banks of the Tamasā. They are tawny with the washed saffron paste applied to the breasts of the city women.
Having beheld the lovely Sarayū river, you shall go to the city of Ayodhyā. Seeing you, our mothers, together with Maithilī, will be filled with joy and will inquire after the welfare of us both.
And Bharata was exceedingly pleased.
"You have reported that the enemy has been slain, Vibhīṣaṇa consecrated,
and Sugrīva won as an ally."
Having quickly heard your words, all the citizens who were about to arrive will experience supreme joy;
and knowing this, Bharata will certainly come together with them, facing you directly.
"Once you have gone by this path, we too shall follow;
I have gained confidence now that you have returned to my presence. When he had departed, Rāma, having grasped his purpose, [confronted] Sugrīva and the Rākṣasa.
He said: "Tomorrow you two, together with me, shall go to the city.
There you shall behold my three mothers, their inner selves satisfied;
and you shall attain the ultimate friendship that rests upon Bharata."
"We shall not be so distressed by the pain of separation, nor shall we experience such exhaustion born of parting from you both;
thus, O monkey and rākṣasa, you two have served to bring me joy."
"If you two strive to go with me tomorrow morning," then Rāma and the monkey descendant of Pulastya spoke these words to him:
"O Kākutstha, this is a great favor."
May we go together with you;
may we both grant our consent to you, even if we were to attain the sovereignty of the lord of gods, for we cannot endure separation from you.
"What indeed have you bestowed as a dwelling place?
Then, having passed the night with conversation, you ascended the Puṣpaka chariot along with your armies.
Setting out with great force, they agitated the unfathomable waters of the ocean;
[they crossed] the Setu, Mahendra,
Malaya, and Vindhya mountains.
Rāma proceeded while recounting to his beloved the Mount Ṛṣyamūka together with Mālyavat, as well as Lake Pampā situated within the Daṇḍaka forest.
These are those very horizons adorned by the community of sages.
This is that Citrakūṭa mountain, its forests stirred;
this is the Gaṅgā, beautiful with its vast and lovely banks.
Bestowing these upon Maithilī, the son of Raghu rejoiced.
O fair-limbed one, here are those very trees whose flower-tops are crowded with the humming of swarms of bees, which were submerged and covered by the flooding of the melting cool waters.

The forest edges, delightful to the eye, are seen being enjoyed by the city folk. I recognize this place as our former home; this beloved Ayodhyā is even more dear to me, she who is beheld from afar with all her gods gratified by various offered oblations.
"This is that very place,
O Sītā, where we two departed at the end of the night for the depths of the forest, leaving behind all the people of the city weeping, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa who maintained his fortitude."
Then, filling the entire world with the sound of musical instruments, making the earth tremble on all sides by the powerful strides of his elephants which resembled the lords of mountains,
Bharata— his eyes filled with tears of joy, accompanied by his ministers, the ladies of the inner court, and his mothers— arrived, bowing low along with Māruti. Then,
surrounded by the agitated citizens and holding a radiant fly-whisk in his hand, Bharata approached.
Welcomed by his elders, the twice-born, and those worthy of praise, the joy of the Raghus entered the city.
Then, having established supreme confidence among the people and consecrated Bharata as the crown prince,
the lord of subjects, having completed the preparations for the rite, set about performing the horse sacrifice.
This work, which displays the manifold path to liberation attained through the excellent treatises of those who desire and proclaim [the truth],
always brings victory to people, just as a well-aimed divine weapon does in battle.
This composition is like a lamp for those whose eyes are the characteristics of the Word.
Without grammar, this [work] would be like a hand to the blind or like indignation to the sightless.
This poem is accessible through its commentary and is a sufficient festival for the wise; and because it is dear to the learned, I have destroyed the wicked clouds that obscure it.
This poem was composed by me in Valabhī, which is protected by the illustrious King Śrīdharasena;
may it bring glory to that king,
for he is a ruler of the earth who bestows affection upon his subjects.
